lessons.title: Printing in Java
objectives: print a line of text with System.out.println
stack several printed lines to build a screen
keep the cursor on the same line with System.out.print

steps.instruction: We're building a game's title screen.

points.label: title, menu, prompt
points.text: A title at the top, two choices, and a line asking the player to pick one.

points.label: "*** DUNGEON QUEST ***"
points.text: Every line a program has ever printed is just text it was told to print, character for character.

points.label: System.out.println
points.text: One command builds the entire screen. You meet its no-newline twin later in the lesson.

steps.instruction: This is the command that puts text on the screen.
steps.code: System.out.println("*** DUNGEON QUEST ***");

points.label: System.out.println
points.text: Spelled exactly like that. Capital S, everything else lowercase, no spaces.

points.label: the quotes
points.text: Whatever sits between the double quotes is what appears. Java does not read it — it just prints it.

points.label: the quotes vanish
points.text: They mark where the text starts and stops. They never show up in the output.

points.label: the semicolon
points.text: Ends the instruction. Every line like this needs one.

steps.instruction: Rename the game to anything you like.
steps.code: System.out.println("*** DUNGEON QUEST ***");
steps.hint: Change the text between the quotes.
steps.after: Your game, your title.
skills: print a line of text with System.out.println

steps.instruction: Add the menu. Each println starts a new line.

points.label: three commands
points.text: Three printlns, three lines. They run top to bottom, in order.

points.label: ln
points.text: The ln on the end means "then move to the next line". That is why they stack instead of running together.

points.label: the spaces count
points.text: The two spaces before 1. are inside the quotes, so they get printed too. That is how the menu is indented.

steps.instruction: print and println differ by one thing: the line ending.

sides.label: print
sides.code:
System.out.print("Hi");
System.out.print("Bye");

sides.label: println
sides.code:
System.out.println("Hi");
System.out.println("Bye");

points.label: print
points.text: Leaves the line open, so Bye continues on it.

points.label: println
points.text: Ends the line, so Bye starts a new one.

skills: keep the cursor on the same line with System.out.print

steps.instruction: A gap under the title makes it readable.

points.label: println("")
points.text: Nothing between the quotes, so it prints nothing — then moves to the next line anyway.
Zero characters printed, and the line still ends. That is a blank line.

points.label: title, gap, menu
points.text: Same words, easier to read. Where the gaps go is a decision you make, not something Java does for you.

steps.instruction: The last line is different — the player types right after it.
steps.output:
*** DUNGEON QUEST ***

  1. New game
  2. Quit

Choose 1-2:

points.label: print, no ln
points.text: Prints and STAYS on the line. The cursor waits right after the text.

points.label: Choose 1-2: 2
points.text: print keeps the answer on the question line. println would drop it below.

points.label: the space
points.text: The space after the colon is inside the quotes, so the answer will not touch the question mark.

points.label: print vs println
points.text: Identical commands apart from one thing: println ends the line, print leaves it open.

steps.instruction: Two prints in a row this time. What comes out?
steps.why: Neither print ends its line, so all three land on one line. Only the final println ends it.
skills: keep the cursor on the same line with System.out.print

steps.instruction: Run the finished title screen.
steps.after: You built a whole screen out of one command and its no-newline twin.
skills: stack several printed lines to build a screen

steps.instruction: println ends the line. print does not.

points.label: System.out.println
points.text: Capital S, then out, then println all in lowercase. printLine, System.println and bare print do not exist.

points.label: println
points.text: Prints, then ENDS the line.

points.label: print
points.text: Prints, and LEAVES the line open. The next thing continues right after it.

points.label: one / twothree
points.text: Line 1 used println, so it ended. Line 2 used print, so it stayed open — and line 3 landed on the same line as "two".

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.
steps.code: System.out.println("Hello Karel");

questions.prompt: Which one actually prints in Java?
questions.why: println is all lowercase, and it has to be System.out in front. The other three do not exist.

questions.prompt: System.out.println("Hello"); then System.out.println("World"); prints how many lines?
questions.why: Each println ends its own line, so the two words land on separate lines.

skills: print a line of text with System.out.println

steps.instruction: This one will not run. Something is missing.
steps.code: System.out.println(Game over);
steps.solution: System.out.println("Game over");
steps.hint: Text has to be wrapped in double quotes, or Java tries to read it as code.
steps.after: Without quotes Java thinks Game and over are things you defined. They are not.
skills: print a line of text with System.out.println

steps.instruction: Tap the lines in order to make the output below.
steps.hint: print keeps the line open. println closes it.
steps.after: You now control exactly where each line breaks.
skills: keep the cursor on the same line with System.out.print

steps.instruction: Introduce yourself in two lines.
steps.code: // line 1 says your name, line 2 says what you like
steps.target:
My name is Ada.
I like comedy.
steps.solution:
System.out.println("My name is Ada.");
System.out.println("I like comedy.");
steps.hint: Two printlns. Line 1 must contain the word name, line 2 the word like.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.1.5, Welcome Program.
skills: stack several printed lines to build a screen

steps.instruction: Last one: draw this exactly.
steps.code: // four printlns, one per line of the drawing
steps.hint: One println per line. The spaces at the start of each line go inside the quotes.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.1.6, ASCII Art. Lesson done.
skills: stack several printed lines to build a screen

lessons.title: Variables and Types
objectives: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name
use = to put a value in, and change it later
choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: We're building a player card.

points.label: the card
points.text: Five facts about one player: their name, their level, their health, their rank, and whether they are online.

points.label: name, level, health
points.text: Text, a whole number, and a half. Three different types.

points.label: a variable
points.text: A labelled box that holds one fact. You put a value in once, then use the label wherever you need it.

points.label: one box at a time
points.text: The card grows on screen as each new type arrives, and by the last step you have built all five.

steps.instruction: First fact: the name. Text goes in a String.

points.label: String name
points.text: The type goes in FRONT of the name you choose. That is what creates the box.

points.label: = "Ada"
points.text: The = does not mean "equals". It means "put this in". The text goes into the box.

points.label: String
points.text: Capital S. Holds text of any length, in double quotes.

points.label: the + sign
points.text: Joins text together. "Name:   " is spelled out by you; name is fetched from the box. The + glues them into one line.

points.label: no quotes on name
points.text: With quotes, "name" would print the word. Without them, Java goes and gets what is inside the box.

steps.instruction: Put your own name on the card.
steps.hint: Change the text inside the quotes on line 1.
steps.after: One edit changed the card. The label on the left stayed put.
skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

steps.instruction: Next fact: the level. Whole numbers go in an int.

points.label: int level
points.text: Same shape as before: type, name, =, value.

points.label: int
points.text: Whole numbers only. 7, 0, -3. No decimal point.

points.label: no quotes
points.text: 7 is a number, so it needs no quotes. "7" with quotes would be text.

points.label: two boxes, two lines
points.text: Each new variable adds one more line to the card.

steps.instruction: The player levels up. Changing a box is not the same as making one.

points.label: int level = 7;
points.text: Type in FRONT, so this MAKES the box. This is called declaring, and you do it once.

points.label: level = 8;
points.text: No type. The box already exists, so this only puts a new value in.

points.label: the 7 is gone
points.text: A box holds one value. Putting 8 in throws the 7 away — it does not add up.

points.label: int level = 8;
points.text: Writing that second line WITH the type would be an error: you cannot make the same box twice.

steps.instruction: What does this print?
steps.why: The second line replaces what is in the box. It does not add — 7 and 8 never meet.
skills: use = to put a value in, and change it later

steps.instruction: Next fact: health. Half a heart will not fit in an int.
steps.output:
=== PLAYER CARD ===
Name:   Ada
Level:  7
Health: 2.5

points.text: Health is 2.5 hearts. An int has nowhere to keep the .5, so the value simply will not fit in one.

points.label: double
points.text: Works exactly like int, but it keeps the decimal part.

points.label: int or double
points.text: int for things you COUNT — levels, lives, coins. double for things you MEASURE — health, height, money.

points.label: double h = 3;
points.text: Allowed. A double can hold a whole number perfectly well; it just displays it as 3.0.

steps.instruction: This one refuses to run. Fix the type.
steps.code:
int health = 2.5;
System.out.println("Health: " + health);
steps.solution:
double health = 2.5;
System.out.println("Health: " + health);
steps.hint: 2.5 has a decimal point. Which type keeps that?
steps.after: Java refused rather than quietly losing your .5. That refusal is it protecting you.
skills: choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: Next fact: the rank, a single letter.
steps.output:
=== PLAYER CARD ===
Name:   Ada
Level:  7
Health: 2.5
Rank:   A

points.label: char
points.text: Exactly ONE character. A letter, a digit, a symbol — one.

points.label: 'A'
points.text: SINGLE quotes. 'A' is a char. "A" with double quotes would be a String.

points.label: char vs String
points.text: A rank is always exactly one letter, so char states that precisely. A name could be any length, so it stays a String.

steps.instruction: Last fact: are they online? That is a yes or a no.
steps.output:
=== PLAYER CARD ===
Name:   Ada
Level:  7
Health: 2.5
Rank:   A
Online: true

points.label: boolean
points.text: Holds only true or false. Nothing else is allowed in the box.

points.label: lowercase, no quotes
points.text: true, not True, and not "true" — quotes would make it text.

points.label: five facts, five types
points.text: Every type was chosen because of what it had to hold, not because a list said so.

steps.instruction: Which type holds each value?
steps.why: Whole number → int. Decimal → double. One character in single quotes → char. Text in double quotes → String. true/false → boolean.
skills: choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: Four parts, one order: type, name, =, value.

points.label: four parts
points.text: Every declaration is: TYPE, NAME, =, VALUE. In that order, ending in a semicolon.

points.label: declare once
points.text: The type appears only the first time. After that, just name = value.

points.label: capitals matter
points.text: level and Level are two different boxes. Java will not guess what you meant.

points.label: quotes decide the type
points.text: "A" is a String. 'A' is a char. A is a variable name. Same letter, three meanings.

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a type Java has?
questions.why: int, double, char and boolean are all built into Java. apple is just a word — Java has never heard of it.

questions.prompt: Which line both MAKES a box and puts a value in?
questions.why: It has all four parts: type, name, =, value. The second only changes an existing box; the third has no name; the fourth is just text.

skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

steps.instruction: Put the right type in front of each name.
steps.hint: Text in double quotes, then a whole number.
steps.after: Type in front, every time.
skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

steps.instruction: This will not run. Look carefully at the capitals.
steps.code:
int Level = 7;
System.out.println("Level:  " + level);
steps.solution:
int level = 7;
System.out.println("Level:  " + level);
steps.hint: Level and level are two different names as far as Java is concerned.
steps.after: One capital letter is enough to break it. Java never guesses.
skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

steps.instruction: a = b copies the value. Follow it.

questions.prompt: after line 3, a = ?
questions.why: a = b copies what is currently in b, which is 2.

questions.prompt: after line 4, a = ?
questions.why: Still 2. Copying took the value, not the box — changing b later does nothing to a.

skills: use = to put a value in, and change it later

steps.instruction: Fill in the two missing values so it prints the card below.
steps.hint: Text needs double quotes. A whole number needs none.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.2.5, Answering Questions.
skills: choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: Last one: store the year in an int, then print the sentence.
steps.code: // declare an int called year, then print it
steps.solution:
int year = 2026;
System.out.println("The current year is " + year);
steps.hint: Type, name, =, value. Then join text and the box with a +.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.2.4, Our First Integer. Lesson done.
skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

lessons.title: User Input
objectives: read what the user types with readLine
choose the reader that matches the type you need
store a typed value in a variable and use it later

steps.instruction: Your player card always says Ada. A real game asks the player.

points.label: String name = "Ada";
points.text: Every value on the card was typed by YOU, into the code. To play as someone else you would have to edit the program and save it again.

points.label: print, then wait
points.text: It shows the question, then stops. Nothing runs until the player types a line and presses enter.

points.label: into a variable
points.text: What they typed has to be stored, or it is gone the moment the next line runs.

steps.instruction: readLine does all three things in one line.
steps.code:
String name = readLine("Your name? ");
System.out.println("Welcome, " + name + "!");

points.label: readLine("Your name? ")
points.text: Prints the question "Your name? ", then stops the program and waits for the player to type a line and press enter.

points.label: "Your name? "
points.text: The question goes INSIDE the brackets. You do not print it yourself on a separate line — readLine prints it for you.

points.label: String name =
points.text: Whatever the player typed comes back out of readLine and is stored in name. From this line onwards, name holds their answer.

points.label: "Welcome, " + name
points.text: name is used further down, so the greeting is different for every player. That is the entire point.

steps.instruction: Your turn — type a name, any name, and run it.
steps.code:
String name = readLine("Your name? ");
System.out.println("Welcome, " + name + "!");
steps.after: Whatever you typed is what came back out. Nothing about the name is written in the code.
skills: read what the user types with readLine

steps.instruction: Three things happened, in order.

points.label: 1. The question printed
points.text: "Your name? " appeared, with no line break after it, so your answer landed on the same line.

points.label: 2. The program stopped
points.text: It waited. Java did not run the next line until it had a full line of input from you.

points.label: 3. Your text went into name
points.text: readLine handed back exactly the characters you typed, and the = put them into the name box.

points.label: a different name
points.text: Go back a step and type something else. The code does not change; the output does.

steps.instruction: Now two questions. Type a name and a starting level.
steps.after: Two reads, two answers, in the order the code asks for them.
skills: store a typed value in a variable and use it later

steps.instruction: readInt was used for the level, not readLine. That matters.

points.label: readInt("Starting level? ")
points.text: Asks the question the same way, but hands back a whole number instead of text.

points.label: int level =
points.text: A number came back, so it goes in an int. The reader decides the type, and the box has to match it.

points.label: level + 1
points.text: level is a number, so this adds. readLine gives "7", and "7" + 1 glues into "71".

points.label: readDouble / readBoolean
points.text: The same pattern for a decimal and for true/false. Four readers, one per type of answer.

steps.instruction: Build the whole character creator. Fill in all four.
steps.after: Four questions, four types, four variables — and a card that belongs to whoever is playing.
skills: choose the reader that matches the type you need

steps.instruction: Four readers, one per type of answer.

points.label: readLine
points.text: Hands back a String. Use it for names, words, sentences — anything that is text.

points.label: readInt
points.text: Hands back an int. Use it for counts and whole numbers you will calculate with.

points.label: readDouble
points.text: Hands back a double. Use it for measurements that can have a decimal point.

points.label: readBoolean
points.text: Hands back a boolean. The player types the word true or the word false.

points.label: There is no readChar
points.text: Those four are the complete set. A single character comes back as a String.

points.label: The prompt is an argument
points.text: It goes inside the brackets, and it does not end its line — which is why the typed answer appears right beside it.

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a real input method?
questions.why: Java on CodeHS gives you exactly four readers, and readChar is not one of them. To read a single character you use readLine and get a String back.

questions.prompt: int n = readInt("Number "); then println(n). The player types 10. What appears after the question?
questions.why: readInt hands back the number 10 itself, and println prints what is inside n. The variable name is not printed, and there are no quotes because it is a number, not text.

skills: choose the reader that matches the type you need

steps.instruction: Match each reader to the type it hands back.
steps.why: The reader you pick decides the type that comes back, and that decides the box you must store it in.
skills: choose the reader that matches the type you need

steps.instruction: A name is text, but this asks for a number. Fix the reader.
steps.code:
String name = readInt("Your name? ");
System.out.println("Hi, " + name + "!");
steps.solution:
String name = readLine("Your name? ");
System.out.println("Hi, " + name + "!");
steps.hint: readInt hands back an int, and an int will not fit in a String box. Which reader hands back text?
steps.after: The reader must match the kind of answer, and the box must match the reader. Both, every time.
skills: choose the reader that matches the type you need

steps.instruction: Pick the reader that fits each question.
steps.hint: An age is a whole number. A price like 9.99 is not.
steps.after: The box on the left already tells you which reader belongs on the right.
skills: choose the reader that matches the type you need

steps.instruction: Last one: ask three questions, then print the three answers.
steps.code: // ask about food, colour and movie, then print all three
steps.target:
What is your favorite food? pasta
What is your favorite color? green
What is your favorite movie? Moana
pasta
green
Moana
steps.hint: Three readLine calls storing three answers, then three printlns. The questions are "What is your favorite food? ", "What is your favorite color? " and "What is your favorite movie? ".
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.3.4, About You. Lesson done.
skills: store a typed value in a variable and use it later

lessons.title: Arithmetic Expressions
objectives: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations
predict the result of whole-number division
use the remainder operator to find what is left over

steps.instruction: Your party just found a pile of loot. Time to split it.

points.label: 17 coins, 5 players
points.text: How many does each player get, and how many are left over that cannot be split evenly?

points.label: 0.4 of a coin
points.text: You cannot hand out part of a coin, so the answer has to be a whole number — and Java has a firm opinion about how to get one.

points.label: + - * first
points.text: The ordinary arithmetic comes first, then the splitting.

steps.instruction: Java does maths with the symbols you already know.

points.label: + and -
points.text: Add and subtract, exactly as you would expect.
Multiply. A star, not an × — there is no × key on a keyboard.

points.label: gold + found
points.text: Uses the values inside the two boxes: 50 + 12.

points.label: gold is still 50
points.text: Printing gold + found works out an answer and prints it. It does not put anything back into gold.

steps.instruction: Buying two potions and a sword — order matters.

points.label: 2 * potion + sword
points.text: Two potions at 3 gold, plus one sword at 10.

points.label: * goes first
points.text: Multiply and divide happen before add and subtract — the same rule as maths class.
Anything inside brackets is worked out before everything else, so brackets are how you override the order.

steps.instruction: Brackets added. Now what?
steps.why: The brackets force potion + sword first: 3 + 10 is 13, then 2 * 13 is 26. Same numbers, different answer.
skills: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations

steps.instruction: 17 coins between 5 players. Java says 3, not 3.4.

points.text: In ordinary maths this is 3.4. Java gives 3.

points.label: int / int
points.text: Two ints give an int. 3.4 loses the .4 — chopped, not rounded.

points.label: 3 coins each
points.text: Which is genuinely the right answer here: you cannot hand out 0.4 of a coin.

points.label: 2 coins unaccounted for
points.text: Java dropped them silently. % gets them back.

steps.instruction: What does this print?
steps.code: System.out.println(9 / 2);
steps.why: Two whole numbers, so the answer stays whole. 4.5 chops down to 4 — it never rounds up.
skills: predict the result of whole-number division

steps.instruction: % gives you exactly what was left over.

points.text: The remainder. Read it as "what is left after dividing".
5 goes into 17 three times, using 15 coins. 2 are left. So 2.
A remainder of 0 means it divided evenly. That is how you will test for even numbers later.

steps.instruction: One more thing: changing a number you already have.

points.label: gold += 12
points.text: Short for gold = gold + 12. Take what is in the box, add 12, put it back.

points.label: gold++
points.text: Short for gold = gold + 1. Adds exactly one.
The same pattern: gold -= 5 means gold = gold - 5, and *= and /= work the same way.

points.label: i++
points.text: Every for loop you write from lesson 3.9 onwards ends in i++. This line is where that syntax comes from.

steps.instruction: Run the finished loot split.
steps.after: Three each, two in the pot. That is the whole job done with / and %.
skills: use the remainder operator to find what is left over

points.text: Two whole numbers, whole answer: 3. The .5 is gone, not rounded.
One decimal is enough to make the whole thing decimal: 3.5.
The remainder: 1. That is the .5 you lost, expressed as what was left.

points.label: 2 + 3 * 4 is 14
points.text: Brackets first, then * / %, then + -. Operations of equal rank run left to right, which is why 7 / 20 * 100 divides before it multiplies.

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.
steps.code:
int a = 150;
int b = 100;

questions.prompt: What is 150 % 100?
questions.why: 100 goes into 150 once, using 100. 50 is left over.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a Java arithmetic operator?
questions.why: Java uses + - * / and %. The # symbol means nothing to it.

skills: use the remainder operator to find what is left over

steps.instruction: Fill it in so it splits 17 into boxes of 5.
steps.hint: First how many fit, then what refuses to fit.
steps.after: / and % are a pair. You will almost always want both.
skills: predict the result of whole-number division

steps.instruction: One decimal in the sum. What now?
steps.code: System.out.println(9 / 2.0);
steps.why: 2.0 is a decimal, so Java keeps the decimal answer. Compare with 9 / 2, which gave 4.
skills: predict the result of whole-number division

steps.instruction: Last one: work out what a pyramid weighs. Each block is 2.5 tons.
steps.code: // ask how many blocks, then print the weight
steps.target:
Enter the number of blocks used to build the pyramid: 3
The pyramid weighs 7.5 tons
steps.solution:
int blocks = readInt("Enter the number of blocks used to build the pyramid: ");
System.out.println("The pyramid weighs " + (blocks * 2.5) + " tons");
steps.hint: Read the count with readInt, multiply by 2.5, and join it into the sentence. Keep the brackets around the sum.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.4.5, Weight of a Pyramid. Lesson done.
skills: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations

lessons.title: Casting
objectives: use (double) so whole-number division keeps its decimal
use (int) to turn a decimal into a whole number
round to the nearest whole number using casting

steps.instruction: Your character has 7 XP. The next level needs 20.

points.label: Progress: 35%
points.text: The share of the way to the next level, shown as a whole number.
Seven out of twenty, as a percentage. Straightforward arithmetic.

points.label: 7 / 20 * 100 gives 0
points.text: Java prints 0, not 35.

points.label: (double) and (int)
points.text: Two casts, doing opposite jobs. One keeps a decimal the division would destroy; the other removes it again for display.

steps.instruction: 7 XP out of 20, times 100. Java prints 0.

points.label: 7 / 20 first
points.text: Equal precedence, so left to right. The division goes first.

points.label: both are ints
points.text: 7 / 20 = 0.35. As ints, that is 0.

points.label: then 0 * 100
points.text: 0 * 100 = 0. The answer was already lost.

points.label: Java is not broken
points.text: This is what int division always does.

steps.instruction: Casting tells Java to treat a value as a different type.

points.label: (double)
points.text: The type you want, in brackets, in front of the value. Here it turns 7 into 7.0.
7.0 / 20 = 0.35. One decimal keeps the decimal.

points.label: (double) xp
points.text: Cast one side. Java converts the other.
A double, so it shows a decimal point. Turning that into a plain 35 is coming.

steps.instruction: Same cast, moved. What does this print?
steps.why: The brackets make xp / needed happen FIRST, as two ints — that is already 0. Casting 0 gives 0.0. The cast arrived too late to save anything.
skills: use (double) so whole-number division keeps its decimal

steps.instruction: A cast only reaches what comes immediately after it.

points.label: (double) x / y
points.text: Works. (double) (x / y) does not — the cast has to reach the division before it happens.

points.label: (double) (7 / 20)
points.text: 7 / 20 = 0 first. (double) 0 = 0.0. Too late.

points.label: (double) x
points.text: A cast applies only to the thing immediately after it. Brackets change what that thing is.

points.label: (double) xp / needed
points.text: Put the cast on the first value, so it reaches the division. Not around the whole sum.

steps.instruction: 35.0 has a decimal point. The bar should read 35.
steps.code:
double percent = 35.9;
System.out.println((int) percent);

points.label: (int)
points.text: Turns a decimal into a whole number.

points.label: 35.9 gives 35
points.text: Chops the decimal. 35.999 also gives 35.

points.label: even 35.999
points.text: Still 35. Casting never looks at how close it was.

points.label: (int) 9.9 is 9
points.text: The exact question the quiz asks. Not 10.

steps.instruction: To round properly, nudge it first.
steps.code:
double percent = 37.5;
System.out.println((int) (percent + 0.5));

points.label: + 0.5 then chop
points.text: 37.5 + 0.5 is 38.0, which chops to 38. Rounded up, using only chopping.

points.label: 37.4 + 0.5 is 37.9
points.text: Chops to 37. Correct.

points.label: exactly .5 goes up
points.text: That is the rule you were taught in maths, and this reproduces it.

points.label: (int) (percent + 0.5)
points.text: The + 0.5 must happen before the chop, so it needs its own brackets inside the cast.

steps.instruction: Run the finished XP readout.
steps.after: Both casts, doing different jobs: one to keep the decimal, one to get rid of it.
skills: round to the nearest whole number using casting

steps.instruction: (int) chops. (double) must arrive before the division.

points.label: (int) and (double)
points.text: Taking a value of one type and treating it as another. That is the entire definition.

points.label: (int) 9.9 is 9
points.text: Chops. Never rounds. This is the single most asked casting question.

points.label: (double) 9 / 2 is 4.5
points.text: The cast reaches the 9 before the division, so the division is decimal.

points.label: (double) (9 / 2) is 4.0
points.text: The brackets divide first as ints — 4 — and then convert. Same symbols, different answer.

steps.instruction: One decimal point changes the answer.

sides.label: both ints
sides.code: System.out.println(7 / 2);

sides.label: one double
sides.code: System.out.println(7.0 / 2);

points.text: Two ints, so the answer must be an int. 3.5 becomes 3.
One side is a decimal, so the answer keeps its decimal.

skills: use (double) so whole-number division keeps its decimal

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.
steps.code:
double d = 9.9;
int i = (int) d;

questions.prompt: What is casting in Java?
opts: Turning a value of one type into another type
A way to print to the screen
What Karel does when she breaks her leg
A way to get user input
questions.why: That is the whole idea: the value stays, the type it is treated as changes.

questions.prompt: What does (int) 9.9 evaluate to?
questions.why: Casting to int chops everything after the decimal point. It does not round, so 9.9 gives 9, not 10.

skills: use (int) to turn a decimal into a whole number

steps.instruction: Fill it in so 3.4 rounds to 3 — and 3.6 would round to 4.
steps.code:
double rating = 3.4;
System.out.println((int) (rating ⟦1⟧ 0.5));
steps.hint: Nudge it up by half, then let the chop decide.
steps.after: 3.4 + 0.5 is 3.9, which chops to 3. Not enough of a nudge to reach 4 — exactly right.
skills: round to the nearest whole number using casting

steps.instruction: Read a decimal and print it as a whole number.
steps.code:
double myDouble = readDouble("Please input your double: ");
// print the int version
steps.solution:
double myDouble = readDouble("Please input your double: ");
System.out.println((int) myDouble);
steps.hint: Put (int) in front of it. No rounding — just the cast.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.5.4, Casting to an Int.
skills: use (int) to turn a decimal into a whole number

steps.instruction: Read two whole numbers and divide them — but keep the decimal.
steps.hint: Cast the FIRST one, before the division happens. 3 / 4 as ints would be 0.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.5.5, Casting to a Double.
skills: use (double) so whole-number division keeps its decimal

steps.instruction: Last one: round a film rating to the nearest whole star.
steps.code:
double movieRating = readDouble("Please enter a movie rating: ");
// round it and print "Rating rounded: N"
steps.target:
Please enter a movie rating: 3.5
Rating rounded: 4
steps.hint: Add 0.5, cast to int, then join it into the sentence.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.5.8, Movie Ratings. Lesson done.

lessons.title: Booleans
objectives: create boolean variables that hold true or false
tell a boolean apart from text, a character and a number
read a true/false answer from the user

steps.instruction: A game is full of facts that are simply yes or no.

points.label: the panel
points.text: Is the player alive? Do they have the key? Is the quest finished? We are building that status screen.

points.label: not a number
points.text: None of these is a count or a measurement. There is no "3 alive". It is yes or no, and nothing else.

points.label: true or false
points.text: A yes/no fact is so common that Java gives it a type of its own, with exactly two possible values.

points.label: doorLocked
points.text: From 3.11, every decision starts from a value like this.

steps.instruction: boolean holds one of exactly two values.

points.label: boolean
points.text: The type. Same four parts as always: type, name, =, value.

points.label: true
points.text: One of only two values it can ever hold. The other is false.

points.label: lowercase, no quotes
points.text: true, not True and not "true". Java is strict about this.

points.label: alive
points.text: Naming it like a yes/no question makes the code read like English.

steps.instruction: The player just died. Make the panel say so.
steps.hint: There is only one other value a boolean can hold.
steps.after: Two values, and you have now used both.
skills: create boolean variables that hold true or false

steps.instruction: Three facts, three booleans.
steps.output:
=== STATUS ===
Alive:      true
Has key:    false
Quest done: true

points.label: one box per fact
points.text: Each yes/no answer needs its own boolean. They do not share.

points.label: false is a real value
points.text: hasKey = false is not "empty" or "unset". It is a definite no.

points.label: alive, no key, quest done
points.text: Three words describe the player completely.

steps.instruction: true and "true" both print as true. They are different types.

points.label: true and "true"
points.text: Both print true. Quotes never appear in output, so you cannot tell them apart by looking.

points.label: true
points.text: A boolean. Java understands it as a yes and can reason with it.

points.label: "true"
points.text: A String. Four letters that happen to spell true. Java cannot make a decision from it.

points.label: 'T' and 10.1
points.text: 'T' is a char — one character in single quotes. 10.1 is a double. Neither is a boolean; only bare true and false are.

steps.instruction: Which type is each value?
steps.why: Bare true/false → boolean. Double quotes → String. Single quotes around one character → char. A decimal → double.
skills: tell a boolean apart from text, a character and a number

steps.instruction: Let the player answer it themselves.
steps.output:
Did you find the key? true
=== STATUS ===
Has key:    true

points.label: readBoolean
points.text: The fourth reader from the input lesson. It hands back true or false.

points.label: they type the word
points.text: The player types true or false. Anything else is not an answer to a yes/no question.

points.label: box matches reader
points.text: readBoolean gives a boolean, so it goes in a boolean. Same rule as always.

steps.instruction: A boolean is true or false — and nothing else is.

points.label: what it is
points.text: A boolean is a true-or-false value. Not a number, not a character, not text.

points.label: exactly two
points.text: true and false. There is no third option and no "empty".

points.label: "true", 't', 10.1
points.text: A String, a char and a double. Not one of them is a boolean, however much "true" looks like one.

points.label: what it is for
points.text: Storing a yes/no fact, and — from the next lesson on — deciding what the program does.

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.
steps.code:
boolean alive = true;
boolean hasKey = false;

questions.prompt: What is a boolean in Java?
questions.why: That is the whole type: two values, true and false.

questions.prompt: Which of these IS a boolean?
questions.why: Bare true is the boolean. "true" is a String, 'F' is a char, and 10.1 is a double.

skills: tell a boolean apart from text, a character and a number

steps.instruction: The player unlocks the door. What prints?
steps.why: The second line puts a new value in the box, exactly like any other variable. The true is gone.
skills: create boolean variables that hold true or false

steps.instruction: The box is the wrong type. Fix it.
steps.code:
String hasKey = readBoolean("Did you find the key? ");
System.out.println(hasKey);
steps.target:
Did you find the key? true
true
steps.solution:
boolean hasKey = readBoolean("Did you find the key? ");
System.out.println(hasKey);
steps.hint: What type does readBoolean hand back?
steps.after: Reader and box always have to agree.
skills: read a true/false answer from the user

steps.instruction: Last one: ask whether they like ice cream, then print the answer.
steps.code: // ask with readBoolean, store it, print it
steps.target:
Do you like ice cream? true
true
steps.solution:
boolean likesIceCream = readBoolean("Do you like ice cream? ");
System.out.println(likesIceCream);
steps.hint: The question is "Do you like ice cream? " — mind the space before the closing quote.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.6.4, Ice Cream. Lesson done.
skills: read a true/false answer from the user

lessons.title: Logical Operators
objectives: combine two booleans with && so both must be true
combine two booleans with || so either will do
flip a boolean with !

steps.instruction: A dungeon door. You get through with the key AND enough strength.

points.label: two facts
points.text: hasKey is true or false. strongEnough is true or false. You already know how to store both.

points.label: one answer
points.text: The door needs a single true or false: does it open? That answer has to be built out of the two facts.

points.label: AND, OR, NOT
points.text: Three symbols combine booleans. This lesson is those three and nothing else.

steps.instruction: && is true only when both sides are true.
steps.output:
=== DUNGEON DOOR ===
Has key:       true
Strong enough: true
Door opens:    true

points.text: Two ampersands, no space between them. Read it as "and".

points.label: hasKey && strongEnough
points.text: Both are true here, so the whole expression is true and the door opens.

points.label: the brackets
points.text: Needed — + would otherwise glue before the && runs.

points.label: one false is enough
points.text: Set either fact to false and the door stays shut. && has no tolerance.

steps.instruction: The player is not strong enough yet. Make the door stay shut.
steps.target:
=== DUNGEON DOOR ===
Has key:       true
Strong enough: false
Door opens:    false
steps.hint: Change one of the two facts at the top. Leave the last line alone.
steps.after: Key but no strength, and the door refuses. That is && being strict.
skills: combine two booleans with && so both must be true

steps.instruction: Fill in every combination of && .
steps.why: Exactly one row out of four is true. && is the strict one: everything must hold.
skills: combine two booleans with && so both must be true

steps.instruction: || is true when either side is true.

points.text: Two pipe characters, on the backslash key. Read it as "or".

points.label: hasKey is false
points.text: It does not matter. knowsPassword is true, and || only needs one side.

points.label: || vs everyday "or"
points.text: In English "tea or coffee" usually means one or the other. In Java || is also true when BOTH are true.

steps.instruction: Now the same four combinations with || .
steps.why: Exactly one row out of four is false — the mirror image of &&. || only fails when nothing is true.
skills: combine two booleans with || so either will do

steps.instruction: ! flips a boolean to its opposite.
steps.code:
boolean hasKey = false;
System.out.println("Door is locked: " + !hasKey);

points.text: An exclamation mark in front of the value. Read it as "not".

points.label: !hasKey
points.text: hasKey is false, so !hasKey is true. The door is locked precisely because you have no key.

points.label: !true is false
points.text: And !false is true. It only ever swaps the two values.

points.label: ! runs first
points.text: Before && and ||, the same way * runs before +. So true && !false is true && true, which is true.

steps.instruction: The exact expression the quiz asks about.
steps.code: System.out.println(true && !false);
steps.why: !false is true, so this becomes true && true. Both sides are true, so && gives true.
skills: flip a boolean with !

steps.instruction: && needs all. || needs one. ! swaps.

points.text: True only when BOTH sides are true. One row of four.
True when EITHER side is true, including when both are. Three rows of four.
Turns true into false and false into true.

points.label: order
points.text: ! first, then &&, then ||. Brackets override all of it.

points.label: && is not &
points.text: Two characters, both times. A single & is a different operator you have not been taught.

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.
steps.code:
boolean a = true;
boolean b = false;

questions.prompt: Which of these is a logical operator?
questions.why: ! is NOT. The other logical operators are && and ||. % is the remainder operator — arithmetic, not logic — and ## and ** are not Java at all.

questions.prompt: What does true && !false evaluate to?
questions.why: ! runs first and turns false into true, leaving true && true, which is true.

skills: flip a boolean with !

steps.instruction: Only one operator makes this print false.
steps.hint: One side is false. Which operator refuses to accept that?
steps.after: && fails on a single false. || would have accepted the one true and printed true.
skills: combine two booleans with && so both must be true

steps.instruction: Last one: they ride only if they are tall enough AND old enough.
steps.code: // ask both questions with readBoolean, then print whether they can ride
steps.target:
Tall enough? true
Old enough? true
true
steps.hint: Two readBoolean calls storing tallEnough and oldEnough, then print the two joined with &&. The questions are "Tall enough? " and "Old enough? ".
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.7.4, Roller Coaster. Lesson done.
skills: combine two booleans with && so both must be true

lessons.title: Comparison Operators
objectives: compare two values to get true or false
choose between ==, !=, <, >, <= and >=
store a comparison in a boolean and use it

steps.instruction: Last lesson strongEnough was simply handed to you as true.

points.label: boolean strongEnough = true;
points.text: You typed the answer in. The program never worked anything out.

points.label: what a game has
points.text: A level — a number, like 7 — and a rule: you need at least 5 to get through this door.

points.label: the missing piece
points.text: Something that turns "7 and the rule needs 5" into a plain true or false. That is what a comparison does.

steps.instruction: level >= required is worked out into true or false.
steps.output:
--- DUNGEON DOOR ---
Level:         7
Strong enough: true
Door opens:    true

points.label: level >= required
points.text: Reads as "level is at least required". 7 is at least 5, so this whole thing becomes true.

points.label: boolean strongEnough =
points.text: The comparison produces true or false, so it fits in a boolean — the same kind of box you filled by hand last lesson.

points.label: hasKey && strongEnough
points.text: Unchanged from last lesson. The && does not care that one value was typed and the other was calculated.

points.label: >= not >
points.text: "At least 5" includes 5 itself. Using > would shut the door on a player who is exactly level 5.

steps.instruction: Send in a level 3 player. The door should shut.
steps.target:
--- DUNGEON DOOR ---
Level:         3
Strong enough: false
Door opens:    false
steps.hint: Change only the level on line 1. The comparison works it out from there.
steps.after: 3 is not at least 5, so strongEnough became false and && shut the door.
skills: compare two values to get true or false

steps.instruction: There are six comparisons, and they all give true or false.
steps.output:
true
false
true
false
true
false

points.label: > and <
points.text: Strictly greater, strictly less. 10 > 3 is true; 10 < 3 is false.

points.label: >= and <=
points.text: Greater-or-equal, less-or-equal. 80 >= 80 is true because equal counts.
False. Strictly greater excludes the number itself — this one line is the difference between the two.

points.label: == and !=
points.text: Equal and not-equal. 5 == 5 is true; 5 != 5 is false.

steps.instruction: Where exactly do > and >= differ?
steps.why: They agree everywhere except at exactly 5. That single row is the whole difference, and it is where off-by-one bugs live.
skills: choose between ==, !=, <, >, <= and >=

steps.instruction: == asks a question. = gives an answer.

points.text: TWO equals signs. Asks "are these the same?" and produces true or false.
ONE equals sign. Puts the value on the right into the box on the left. It asks nothing.

points.label: int x = 5;
points.text: Assignment — creating a box and filling it.

points.label: x == 5
points.text: Comparison — a question whose answer is true or false.
Not equal. The ! is the same "not" you met last lesson.

steps.instruction: The exact expression the quiz asks about.
steps.code: System.out.println(80 >= 80);
steps.why: >= is satisfied by being greater OR equal. 80 is equal to 80, so it is true. Only > would be false here.
skills: choose between ==, !=, <, >, <= and >=

steps.instruction: Comparisons join with && exactly like any other booleans.

points.label: points >= 10 && rebounds >= 10 && assists >= 10
points.text: Three separate comparisons, each producing true or false, chained with &&.

points.label: assists is 7
points.text: 7 >= 10 is false, and && needs every part true, so the whole thing is false.

points.label: no brackets needed
points.text: Comparisons are worked out before && , so each >= finishes before the ands combine them.

points.label: tripleDouble
points.text: A name that says what the answer MEANS, so the line that prints it reads like English.

steps.instruction: Six operators, one result type: boolean.

points.text: The complete set. Every one of them produces true or false, never a number.
Not a comparison operator. Java has no such thing — it is the quiz distractor.

points.label: 80 >= 80 is true
points.text: Equal counts for >= and <=. It does not count for > or <.

points.label: = vs ==
points.text: Writing = where you meant == is the most common mistake in this unit.

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.
steps.code: int score = 80;

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a comparison operator?
questions.why: Java compares with > < >= <= == and !=. The ? is not one of them.

questions.prompt: What does 80 >= 80 evaluate to?
questions.why: >= means greater than OR equal to, and 80 equals 80. The answer is the boolean true — not the text "true".

skills: choose between ==, !=, <, >, <= and >=

steps.instruction: A score of exactly 10 must count as enough.
steps.hint: "At least 10" has to include 10 itself.
steps.after: "At least" is always >=. Using > would have excluded exactly 10 and printed false.
skills: choose between ==, !=, <, >, <= and >=

steps.instruction: Last one: a triple double needs at least 10 in all three.
steps.code: // read points, rebounds and assists, then print the verdict
steps.target:
Points? 10
Rebounds? 11
Assists? 12
Got a Triple Double? true
steps.hint: Three readInt calls with the prompts "Points? ", "Rebounds? " and "Assists? ", then chain three >= 10 checks with &&, and print "Got a Triple Double? " + the result.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.8.4, Triple Double. Lesson done.
skills: store a comparison in a boolean and use it

lessons.title: For Loops
objectives: write a for loop that repeats a fixed number of times
control where a loop starts, stops and how far it steps
work out how many times a loop body runs

steps.instruction: The dungeon has 5 floors, and each one needs a line.

points.label: five printlns
points.text: This works. The output is exactly right and nothing here is broken.

points.label: "Floor 1" … "Floor 5"
points.text: Every line is identical apart from one number that goes up by one.

points.label: 8 floors
points.text: Would mean typing three more lines. 100 floors would mean typing 95 more.

points.label: what we want
points.text: To say the repeating line ONCE, and say how many times to do it.

steps.instruction: A for loop says the line once and repeats it.

points.label: int floor = 1
points.text: Where the counter starts. This runs once, before anything else.

points.label: floor <= 5
points.text: Checked before every pass. While it is true the block runs; the moment it is false the loop is over.

points.label: floor++
points.text: Runs after each pass, adding 1 to floor. Without it floor stays 1 and the loop never ends.
Everything inside the braces is what gets repeated. Here that is one println.

steps.instruction: The dungeon just grew. Make it print 8 floors.
steps.target:
Floor 1
Floor 2
Floor 3
Floor 4
Floor 5
Floor 6
Floor 7
Floor 8
steps.hint: Only the number in the middle part changes.
steps.after: One character changed. The five-println version would have needed three whole new lines.
skills: write a for loop that repeats a fixed number of times

steps.instruction: The condition is checked before every pass — including one that fails.
steps.why: Six checks for five passes. After printing Floor 5 the counter becomes 6, the check fails, and the loop stops — so the counter always ends up one past the last value it printed.
skills: work out how many times a loop body runs

steps.instruction: Starting at 0 with < is the other common shape.

points.label: i = 0 … i < 3
points.text: Three passes, printing 0, 1 and 2. It stops before 3, so 3 never appears.

points.label: i = 1 … i <= 3
points.text: Also three passes, printing 1, 2 and 3. Same count, different numbers.

points.label: i = 0 … i <= 3
points.text: FOUR passes. Mixing the two shapes is the off-by-one that catches everyone.

points.label: which to use
points.text: Start at 0 with < when you just need N repeats. Start at 1 with <= when the number itself is being shown, like a floor.

steps.instruction: How many lines does this print?
steps.why: i takes the values 0, 1, 2 and 3 — four passes. It stops at 4 because 4 < 4 is false.
skills: work out how many times a loop body runs

steps.instruction: The counter does not have to go up by one.

points.label: i += 2
points.text: Adds 2 after each pass instead of 1, so the counter lands on 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.

points.label: i++
points.text: Just the shorthand for i += 1. The last part can be any change you like.

points.label: i--
points.text: Counts DOWN. Start high, end low, and the condition becomes something like i >= 1.

points.label: odd numbers
points.text: Starting at 1 and stepping by 2 gives every odd number. Starting at 2 gives every even one.

steps.instruction: Three parts, separated by semicolons, then a block.

points.label: for (start; condition; change)
points.text: Start runs once. Condition is checked before every pass. Change runs after every pass.

points.label: for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++)
points.text: The most common loop in Java: ten passes, i going 0 to 9.

points.label: the counter is local
points.text: An i declared in the for line exists only inside the loop. After the loop it is gone.

points.label: for (int i = 0; i < n; i += 2)
points.text: Steps of 2 up to n gives (n + 1) / 2 passes — the counting question the quiz asks.

steps.instruction: Three the test always asks.

questions.prompt: Why do we use for loops in Java?
opts: To do something if a condition is true
To break out of some block of code
To do something while a condition is true
To repeat something a fixed number of times
questions.why: A for loop is the shape you reach for when you already know the count. Repeating while something stays true is a while loop, which is the next lesson.

questions.prompt: Which for loop correctly prints "hello" 10 times?
questions.why: Start, condition, change — in that order. The second has no condition, the third has them swapped, and the fourth starts at 10 where 10 < 0 is already false, so it runs zero times.

questions.prompt: for (int i = 0; i < n; i += 2) — at most how many passes, in terms of n?
questions.why: i lands on 0, 2, 4 … so it takes every other value below n. For n = 5 that is 0, 2, 4 — three passes, and (5 + 1) / 2 is 3.

skills: work out how many times a loop body runs

steps.instruction: Make it print the even numbers up to 10.
steps.hint: Start on the first even number, then jump over every odd one.
steps.after: Start at 2, step by 2. Starting at 1 with the same step would have given the odds instead.
skills: control where a loop starts, stops and how far it steps

steps.instruction: This one never stops. Tap the line to blame.
steps.why: i = 1 drags the counter back to 1 on every pass, so i++ can never get it past 3. The body is allowed to change the counter, and this is how loops get stuck.
skills: work out how many times a loop body runs

steps.instruction: Print the odd numbers from 1 to 9.
steps.code: // print 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 - one per line
steps.hint: Start at 1 and step by 2.
steps.after: Change the 9 to 99 and you have written CodeHS exercise 3.9.8, Print The Odds.
skills: control where a loop starts, stops and how far it steps

steps.instruction: Last one: a factorial. 4 means 4 * 3 * 2 * 1.
steps.code:
int n = readInt("What number would you like to compute the factorial for? ");
// multiply 1 by every number up to n, then print it
steps.target:
What number would you like to compute the factorial for? 4
24
steps.hint: Start result at 1 — not 0, or everything multiplies to nothing. Then loop i from 1 to n doing result = result * i.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.9.11, Factorial. Lesson done.
skills: write a for loop that repeats a fixed number of times

lessons.title: While Loops
objectives: decide when a while loop fits better than a for loop
trace a while loop until its condition fails
recognise why a while loop never stops

steps.instruction: Last lesson the dungeon had 5 floors. A boss fight has no number.

points.label: 5 floors
points.text: You knew the count before starting, so a for loop fitted.

points.label: a boss
points.text: You swing until its HP reaches 0. How many hits that takes depends on the damage rolls.

points.label: what is needed
points.text: A loop that repeats while something stays true, instead of counting to a number.

steps.instruction: while repeats for as long as its condition holds.
steps.output:
Hit 1: boss at 23
Hit 2: boss at 16
Hit 3: boss at 9
Hit 4: boss at 2
Hit 5: boss at -5
Boss down in 5 hits.

points.label: while (bossHp > 0)
points.text: Checked before every swing. True means swing again.

points.label: bossHp = bossHp - 7
points.text: Each pass takes 7 off. This is what eventually makes the condition false.

points.label: boss at -5
points.text: The last hit overshoots. The loop stops at the next check, not the instant HP hits 0.

points.label: 5 hits
points.text: Never written down anywhere. The loop worked it out.

steps.instruction: Known count, or unknown count.

sides.label: for - you know the count
while - you do not

points.label: for
points.text: Three passes because you asked for three.

points.label: while
points.text: Three passes because that is when hp ran out. You did not choose it.

steps.instruction: This boss has 50 HP. Make the fight run to the end.
steps.target:
Hit 1: boss at 43
Hit 2: boss at 36
Hit 3: boss at 29
Hit 4: boss at 22
Hit 5: boss at 15
Hit 6: boss at 8
Hit 7: boss at 1
Hit 8: boss at -6
Boss down in 8 hits.
steps.hint: Nothing is broken - run it and read how many hits a 50 HP boss takes.
steps.after: Same loop, different number of passes. You changed the data, not the logic.
skills: trace a while loop until its condition fails

steps.instruction: Take away the line that changes bossHp and it never ends.

points.label: no subtraction
points.text: bossHp stays 30 forever, so bossHp > 0 is true forever.

points.label: what happens
points.text: The same line prints until something kills the program. No output is shown here because there is no end to show.

points.label: bossHp = bossHp - 7
points.text: Put that line back and the loop ends. Something inside must move the condition towards false.

steps.instruction: Tap the line that should be changing count.
steps.why: The body prints count but never changes it, so count <= 3 stays true forever. It needs count++ here.
skills: recognise why a while loop never stops

steps.instruction: n starts at 10. What prints?
steps.why: The condition is checked BEFORE the first pass. 10 < 5 is false, so the body never runs once.
skills: trace a while loop until its condition fails

steps.instruction: A while loop can count down as easily as up.

points.label: i--
points.text: Takes 1 off each pass, so i falls 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.

points.label: i >= 1
points.text: At i = 0 this is false and the loop stops, so 0 never prints.

points.label: you write it
points.text: Unlike a for loop, the start and the change are separate lines you place yourself.

steps.instruction: for when you know the count. while when you do not.

points.label: while (condition) { }
points.text: Checked before every pass, including the first. A false condition means zero passes.

points.label: the counter
points.text: You declare it before the loop and change it inside. Nothing is automatic.

points.label: while (true)
points.text: Never false on its own. It runs forever unless something inside stops it.

points.label: either works
points.text: Anything a for loop does a while loop can do. Pick the one that states your intent.

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.

questions.prompt: Why do we use while loops in Java?
opts: To repeat something a fixed number of times
To repeat some code while a condition is true
To do something if a condition is true
To break out of some block of code
questions.why: A while loop is the shape for "keep going until this stops being true". A fixed count is a for loop.

questions.prompt: What will while(true) { System.out.println("Hello"); } do?
opts: Print Hello until the program receives user input
Print Hello in an infinite loop
questions.why: true is never false, and nothing inside stops it, so it prints forever.

skills: recognise why a while loop never stops

steps.instruction: Make the countdown stop at 1.
steps.hint: It must keep going while i is still at least 1, and i has to fall.
steps.after: Condition and change work as a pair. Get one wrong and it either stops early or never stops.
skills: trace a while loop until its condition fails
