lessons.title: If Statements
objectives: run a block of code only when a condition is true
use else to handle the other case
use the remainder operator inside a condition

steps.instruction: You have been printing "Door opens: true". A game opens the door.

points.label: Door opens: true
points.text: Everything so far ends by printing a boolean. The program computes an answer and does nothing with it.

points.label: what a game does
points.text: Runs different lines depending on that answer. Open the door, or say it is locked.

points.label: if
points.text: The statement that finally acts on a true or false instead of showing it.

steps.instruction: if runs a block only when the condition is true.
steps.output:
The door swings open.
You walk on.

points.label: if (hasKey && strongEnough)
points.text: The condition is the same boolean you built in 3.8. Nothing new about it.

points.label: the braces
points.text: Only the lines inside { } are skipped when the condition is false.

points.label: "You walk on."
points.text: Outside the braces, so it prints either way.

points.label: no semicolon
points.text: There is no ; after the round brackets. Adding one detaches the block and it always runs.

steps.instruction: Reporting the answer, or acting on it.

sides.label: print the boolean
sides.code:
boolean canOpen = true;
System.out.println("Door opens: " + canOpen);

sides.label: act on it

points.label: left
points.text: Always prints one line, whatever the answer is.

points.label: right
points.text: Prints that line only when canOpen is true. Otherwise nothing.

skills: run a block of code only when a condition is true

steps.instruction: Send in a level 3 player. The door should not open.
steps.hint: Change the level. The condition works the rest out.
steps.after: The block was skipped entirely, and the line after it still ran.
skills: run a block of code only when a condition is true

steps.instruction: else covers the other case.

points.label: else
points.text: Runs when the condition was false. It has no condition of its own.

points.label: exactly one
points.text: One block runs, never both and never neither.

points.label: } else {
points.text: else sits on the closing brace of the if.

steps.instruction: hp is exactly 0. What prints?
steps.why: 0 > 0 is false, so else runs. Zero is where > and >= disagree, and where most off-by-one bugs live.
skills: use else to handle the other case

steps.instruction: A remainder makes a good condition.

points.label: n % 2
points.text: The remainder after dividing by 2. It is 0 or 1, nothing else.

points.label: n % 2 == 0
points.text: Remainder zero means it divided evenly, so n is even.

points.label: 7 % 2 is 1
points.text: Not 0, so the condition is false and else runs.

steps.instruction: 8 is even, but this says odd. Fix the condition.
steps.hint: What remainder does an even number leave when divided by 2?
steps.after: Remainder 0 is even, remainder 1 is odd. It was testing the wrong one.
skills: use the remainder operator inside a condition

steps.instruction: else if checks the next thing only if the last one failed.

points.label: top to bottom
points.text: Java stops at the first condition that is true.
Not >= 90, not >= 80, so it falls through to else.

points.label: order matters
points.text: Put >= 80 first and every score above 90 would print B.

steps.instruction: if (condition) { }, then optionally else.

points.label: if (…) { }
points.text: Round brackets around a boolean, braces around the lines to run.

points.label: else
points.text: Optional. No condition, no brackets.

points.label: else if (…)
points.text: As many as you like, checked in order, first match wins.

points.label: if (x) ;
points.text: A semicolon there ends the if immediately, so the block below always runs. Silent and common.

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.

questions.prompt: Why do we use if statements in Java?
opts: To break out of some block of code
To do something only if a condition is true
To repeat something a fixed number of times
To do something while a condition is true
questions.why: An if runs a block once, or not at all. Repeating while something is true is a while loop.

questions.prompt: Which if statement is written properly?
questions.why: Round brackets around the condition and braces around the block. Java uses neither a colon nor square brackets.

skills: run a block of code only when a condition is true

steps.instruction: Keep the smaller of the two.
steps.hint: Replace min only when b is smaller than what is already there.
steps.after: Assume the first is smallest, then replace it if you find better. That scales to any number of values.
skills: run a block of code only when a condition is true

steps.instruction: Last one: read three numbers and print the smallest.
steps.code: // read three ints, then print the smallest
steps.target:
Enter first number: 10
Enter second number: 15
Enter third number: 20
10
steps.hint: Start with min = a, then two ifs replacing it if b or c is smaller. Prompts are "Enter first number: ", "Enter second number: ", "Enter third number: ".
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.11.5, Find the Minimum. Lesson done.
skills: run a block of code only when a condition is true

lessons.title: Loop-and-a-Half
objectives: use break to leave a loop from the middle
write a while (true) loop that asks once and checks once
stop a loop on a sentinel value

steps.instruction: Today you build the number guessing game.

points.label: the game
points.text: It picks a secret number, you guess, it says "Try again!" until you get it.

points.label: why this one
points.text: It is the coding question on your final exam, and it is CodeHS exercise 3.12.4.

points.label: what is new
points.text: One statement: break. Everything else you already have.

steps.instruction: Here it is with a plain while loop. It works.
steps.output:
Enter your guess: 4
Try again!
Enter your guess: 6
Correct!

points.label: line 1
points.text: Reads a guess before the loop, because while checks its condition first and needs something to check.

points.label: line 4
points.text: Reads the next guess inside the loop.

points.label: the same question twice
points.text: readInt("Enter your guess: ") is written on both lines. Change the wording in one and forget the other, and the game asks two different things.

steps.instruction: Same game, same output. One asks once.

sides.label: plain while - asks twice
sides.output:
Enter your guess: 4
Try again!
Enter your guess: 6
Correct!

sides.label: loop-and-a-half - asks once
sides.output:
Enter your guess: 4
Try again!
Enter your guess: 6
Correct!

points.label: left
points.text: readInt appears on two lines, above the loop and inside it.

points.label: right
points.text: readInt appears once. The check moved into the middle of the loop.

skills: write a while (true) loop that asks once and checks once

steps.instruction: while (true) never stops on its own. break is the exit.
steps.output:
Enter your guess: 4
Try again!
Enter your guess: 6
Correct!

points.label: while (true)
points.text: The condition is always true, so the loop will not end by itself.

points.label: break;
points.text: Leaves the loop immediately, skipping everything below it in the block.

points.label: ask, check, act
points.text: Read the guess, break out if it is right, otherwise print "Try again!" and go round again.

points.label: the half
points.text: On the winning pass only the top half runs. That is where the name comes from.

steps.instruction: break works in any loop. What prints?
steps.why: At i = 3 the break runs before the println, and the whole loop ends. It does not skip one and carry on.
skills: use break to leave a loop from the middle

steps.instruction: Tap the only line that can end this loop.
steps.why: while (true) is never false, so nothing else can stop it. Delete that line and the game runs forever.
skills: use break to leave a loop from the middle

steps.instruction: A sentinel is a value that means "stop".
steps.output:
Number (0 to stop): 5
Number (0 to stop): 7
Number (0 to stop): 0
12

points.text: The sentinel here. Typing it ends the loop instead of adding to the total.

points.label: "Number (0 to stop): "
points.text: The prompt says what the sentinel is. A secret one is a broken program.
5 + 7. The 0 breaks before the addition, so it never joins the total.

points.label: choosing one
points.text: Pick a value that cannot be real data. 0 marks works; 0 degrees does not.

steps.instruction: Fill in the statement that leaves the loop.
steps.target:
Number (0 to stop): 5
5
Number (0 to stop): 0
steps.hint: You want out of the loop entirely, not on to the next pass.
steps.after: break leaves the loop. continue would jump to the next pass and ask again forever.
skills: use break to leave a loop from the middle

steps.instruction: while (true) { ask; if (done) break; act; }

points.label: while (true)
points.text: A loop with no exit condition of its own.

points.label: break;
points.text: The statement that ends a loop early. It ends the loop, not just the pass.

points.label: the shape
points.text: Ask at the top, check in the middle, act at the bottom. The check is what makes it a loop-and-a-half.

points.label: when to use it
points.text: Whenever the thing you test has to be read first. Otherwise a plain while is simpler.

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.

questions.prompt: Which statement can we use inside a loop to end it?
questions.why: break exits the loop immediately. The others are not exit statements.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct loop-and-a-half structure?
questions.why: An always-true loop with the exit test in the middle. The second is an ordinary while; the fourth breaks on the first pass every time.

skills: write a while (true) loop that asks once and checks once

steps.instruction: Last one: the guessing game. The secret is 6.
steps.code:
int secretNumber = 6;
// greet, then keep asking until they get it
steps.target:
I'm thinking of a number between 1 and 10.
See if you can guess the number!
Enter your guess: 4
Try again!
Enter your guess: 3
Try again!
Enter your guess: 6
Correct!
steps.hint: Two greeting lines, then while (true): read the guess, break if it equals secretNumber, otherwise print "Try again!". "Correct!" goes after the loop.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.12.4, and the program your final exam asks for. Lesson done.
skills: write a while (true) loop that asks once and checks once

lessons.title: Short-Circuit Evaluation
objectives: explain why the right-hand side of && or || is sometimes skipped
put a guard on the left so the right side is safe
work out which side of an expression actually runs

steps.instruction: Average damage is total / hits. You missed every swing, so hits is 0.

points.label: totalDamage / hits
points.text: The obvious way to get an average.

points.label: hits = 0
points.text: Dividing an int by zero does not give 0 or infinity. It crashes the program on the spot.

points.label: what is needed
points.text: A way to check hits before the division is allowed to happen.

steps.instruction: && stops at the first false, so the division never runs.

points.label: (hits != 0)
points.text: False, because hits is 0.
Once one side is false the answer is false whatever the other side says, so Java stops there.

points.label: no crash
points.text: totalDamage / hits is never evaluated. The guard on the left protected it.

points.label: not an optimisation
points.text: This is the only reason the program survives. You are relying on it.

steps.instruction: Row 1 only works because of short-circuiting.
steps.why: With hits = 0 the left side is false, so Java never divides. Take the guard away and that row crashes instead of printing false.
skills: explain why the right-hand side of && or || is sometimes skipped

steps.instruction: || stops at the first true, for the same reason.

points.label: (hits == 0)
points.text: True, because hits is 0.
Once one side is true the answer is true, so Java stops and 100 / hits never runs.

points.label: && vs ||
points.text: && gives up on the first false. || gives up on the first true.

steps.instruction: 5 / 0 would crash. Does this?
steps.code: System.out.println(true || (5 / 0 == 0));
steps.why: || found true on the left, so the right side is never evaluated and the division never happens.
skills: explain why the right-hand side of && or || is sometimes skipped

steps.instruction: Does the right-hand side get evaluated?
steps.code: // X is an expression that would crash

questions.prompt: false && X
questions.why: false && anything is false. Java stops.

questions.prompt: true || X
questions.why: true || anything is true. Java stops.

questions.prompt: true && X
questions.why: true tells && nothing yet, so X must run. This one is NOT protected.

skills: work out which side of an expression actually runs

steps.instruction: The guard has to be on the left.

points.label: left to right
points.text: Java always evaluates the left side first.

points.label: (hits != 0) && (100 / hits > 5)
points.text: Safe. The check runs before the division.

points.label: (100 / hits > 5) && (hits != 0)
points.text: Crashes when hits is 0. The division runs before anything checks it.

points.label: (hits != 0) first
points.text: Which side you put first decides whether the program works.

steps.instruction: Pick the operator that keeps this safe.
steps.hint: You need the false on the left to stop everything. Which operator gives up on a false?
steps.after: With || the false on the left is not enough to decide, so the division runs and crashes.
skills: put a guard on the left so the right side is safe

steps.instruction: && stops on false. || stops on true.

points.label: false && X
points.text: X is skipped. The answer is already false.

points.label: true || X
points.text: X is skipped. The answer is already true.

points.label: true && X
points.text: X runs. The answer still depends on it.

points.label: false || X
points.text: X runs, for the same reason.

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.
steps.code: boolean a = true;

questions.prompt: In boolean b = true || (5 / 0 == 0); is 5 / 0 evaluated?
questions.why: || already has a true on the left, so it stops. The division never happens and there is no crash.

questions.prompt: In boolean b = true && (5 / 0 == 0); is 5 / 0 evaluated?
questions.why: A true on the left of && decides nothing, so Java must evaluate the right side — and that one does crash.

skills: work out which side of an expression actually runs

steps.instruction: Last one: say whether one number divides evenly, without crashing on 0.
steps.target:
Enter the dividend: 10
Enter the divisor: 0
10 is not divisible by 0
steps.hint: Put divisor != 0 first, then &&, then the divisibility test. Messages are "X is divisible by Y!" and "X is not divisible by Y".
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.13.4, Divisibility. The guard is the whole exercise.
skills: put a guard on the left so the right side is safe

lessons.title: De Morgan's Laws
objectives: rewrite !(a && b) without the outer not
rewrite !(a || b) without the outer not
check that two boolean expressions mean the same thing

steps.instruction: You can enter with a key AND enough strength. When are you turned away?

points.label: hasKey && strongEnough
points.text: The condition for getting in. You wrote it in 3.7.

points.label: !(hasKey && strongEnough)
points.text: The opposite: turned away. Correct, but it reads as a double negative.

points.label: the other way
points.text: "No key, OR not strong enough." Same rule, no outer !. Turning one into the other is what this lesson is.

steps.instruction: not (A and B) is the same as (not A) or (not B).

points.label: !hasKey || !strongEnough
points.text: The ! moves onto each part, and the && flips to ||.

points.label: "not both"
points.text: is the same as "at least one is missing".

points.label: true
points.text: strongEnough is false, so !strongEnough is true, so the || is true. Turned away.

points.label: the operator must flip
points.text: !hasKey && !strongEnough means something else - it would need BOTH to be missing.

steps.instruction: Both columns, every combination. They match.
steps.why: Four rows, two columns, identical every time. That is what "equivalent" means - not similar, the same in every case.
skills: rewrite !(a && b) without the outer not

steps.instruction: not (A or B) is the same as (not A) and (not B).
steps.output: Stay out of the pool? true

points.label: !canSwim && !hasJacket
points.text: Same recipe: ! onto each part, and this time || flips to &&.

points.label: "neither"
points.text: is the same as "not this AND not that".

points.label: both laws
points.text: not-AND becomes OR. not-OR becomes AND. The operator always flips.

steps.instruction: Same check for the other law.
steps.why: Identical again. Only when both are false is "neither" true.
skills: rewrite !(a || b) without the outer not

steps.instruction: a is true, b is false. What prints?
steps.why: !a is false, !b is true. false || true is true - which matches !(a && b), since a && b is false.
skills: check that two boolean expressions mean the same thing

steps.instruction: Move the ! inwards, flip the operator.

points.label: !(A && B)
points.text: becomes !A || !B

points.label: !(A || B)
points.text: becomes !A && !B

points.label: the flip
points.text: && turns into ||, and || turns into &&. Forgetting this is the whole mistake.

points.label: !(a && b)
points.text: A double negative to read. The flipped form usually says what you mean.

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.
steps.code:
boolean A = true;
boolean B = false;

questions.prompt: Which is equivalent to !(A && B)?
questions.why: The ! goes onto both parts and the && flips to ||. Keeping the && is the usual mistake.

questions.prompt: Which is equivalent to !(A || B)?
questions.why: Same recipe the other way: ! onto both parts, and the || flips to &&.

skills: check that two boolean expressions mean the same thing

steps.instruction: Rewrite !(a && b) without the outer brackets.
steps.hint: The && has to flip.
steps.after: not-AND becomes OR. Every time.
skills: rewrite !(a && b) without the outer not

steps.instruction: Last one: who gets turned away from the ride - in De Morgan form.
steps.target:
Enter your age: 10
Enter your height in inches: 50
true
steps.hint: !(oldEnough && tallEnough) converted is !oldEnough || !tallEnough.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.14.5, Amusement Park. Lesson done.
skills: rewrite !(a && b) without the outer not

lessons.title: Strings
objectives: compare Strings with .equals()
explain why == is the wrong way to compare text
join Strings together with +

steps.instruction: A gate that opens only if the player types the magic word.

points.label: the check
points.text: Read what they typed, compare it with "mellon", open or refuse.

points.label: what you know
points.text: readLine gives a String, and if acts on true or false. Both already yours.
Comparing two Strings with == does not do what you expect. That is this lesson.

steps.instruction: A String is a run of characters in double quotes.

points.label: String
points.text: Capital S. Holds text of any length.

points.label: println(word)
points.text: No quotes, so Java prints what is inside the box: mellon.

points.label: println("word")
points.text: With quotes, so it prints the four letters w-o-r-d.

steps.instruction: Same two words. Different question.

sides.code:
String typed = readLine("Type mellon: ");
System.out.println(typed == "mellon");

sides.label: .equals()
sides.code:
String typed = readLine("Type mellon: ");
System.out.println(typed.equals("mellon"));

points.text: Asks whether they are the same object in memory. The typed one is not.

points.label: .equals()
points.text: Asks whether the characters match. They do.

skills: compare Strings with .equals()

steps.instruction: == compares identity. .equals() compares characters.

points.text: For numbers and booleans this is what you want. For Strings it asks the wrong question.

points.label: .equals()
points.text: Checks the text itself, character by character. Always use this for Strings.

points.label: typed.equals("mellon")
points.text: The variable goes in front, the thing you compare against goes in the brackets.

steps.instruction: No user input this time. What prints?
steps.why: Java reuses identical text written directly in the code, so both names point at the same object and == says true. It looks like == works, which is exactly the trap - the moment the text comes from a user it says false. Use .equals() and you never have to think about it.
skills: explain why == is the wrong way to compare text

steps.instruction: Try the gate. Type mellon, then run it again with something else.
steps.after: .equals() compared the characters you typed against "mellon".
skills: compare Strings with .equals()

steps.instruction: Join first, then compare the whole thing.

points.label: (first + second)
points.text: The brackets join them into one String, "peppermint", before anything is compared.

points.label: .equals(third)
points.text: That whole String is then compared with third.

points.label: without the brackets
points.text: .equals would attach to second alone and ask a different question.

steps.instruction: Text is compared with .equals(). Numbers still use ==.

points.label: String
points.text: A sequence of characters. Not a single character - that is char.

points.label: a.equals(b)
points.text: True when the characters match. The correct way to compare text.

points.label: a == b
points.text: True only when they are the same object. Unreliable for text.

points.label: int x == 5
points.text: Still fine. == is only a problem for Strings.

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.
steps.code: String s = "hello";

questions.prompt: What is a String type in Java?
questions.why: Any amount of text. A single character is char, written in single quotes.

questions.prompt: What is the proper way to compare String values in Java?
questions.why: .equals() compares the characters. == compares object identity, and = assigns.

skills: compare Strings with .equals()

steps.instruction: Fill in the right way to compare.
steps.code:
String typed = readLine("Type cat: ");
System.out.println(typed⟦1⟧);
steps.hint: The text came from the user, so == will say false.
steps.after: .equals() is the only comparison you can trust for text.
skills: compare Strings with .equals()

steps.instruction: Last one: do the first two strings joined make the third?
steps.code: // read three strings, then compare first + second with third
steps.target:
First string? pepper
Second string? mint
Third string? peppermint
pepper + mint is equal to peppermint!
steps.hint: Prompts are "First string? ", "Second string? ", "Third string? ". Then compare (first + second).equals(third) and print either "X + Y is equal to Z!" or "X + Y is not equal to Z!".
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.15.4, Three Strings - the last exercise in the unit. Lesson done.
skills: compare Strings with .equals()

lessons.title: Java Methods
objectives: explain why a method is better than repeating code
create a method and call it

steps.instruction: Every dungeon room prints the same divider above its name.

points.label: two identical lines
points.text: The same println, written twice. Ten rooms would mean ten copies.

points.label: changing it
points.text: Make the divider longer and you have to edit every copy, and you will miss one.

points.label: what we want
points.text: Write the divider once, give it a name, and use the name wherever it is needed.

steps.instruction: A method is a named block of code you can run by name.

To name a block of code and reuse it without repeating it

You enter the cellar.

points.text: Two methods that differ by one word.

steps.output:
You enter the cellar.
You enter the crypt.

points.text: The parameter. Inside the method, room behaves like a variable holding whatever was passed in.

points.label: enter("cellar")
points.text: The call passes "cellar", so room is "cellar" for that run.

points.label: enter("crypt")
points.text: Same method, different value, different sentence.

points.label: one definition

sides.output:
You enter the cellar.
You enter the crypt.

sides.output:
You enter the cellar.
You enter the crypt.

points.text: The sentence exists once. Only the value changes.

steps.instruction: Two words for the two halves.

points.label: parameter
points.text: The name in the definition: String room. It exists only inside the method.

points.label: argument
points.text: The value in the call: "cellar". It is what the parameter is set to.

points.label: in order

steps.output:
You hit the goblin for 7 damage.
You hit the troll for 12 damage.

points.text: Two parameters, separated by a comma. Each has its own type.

points.label: attack(7, "goblin")

points.label: int damage

steps.instruction: public void name(Type param) { } to define. name(value); to call.

points.label: the call

points.label: scope
points.text: A parameter exists only inside its method. run() cannot see room.

lessons.title: Methods and Return Values
objectives: write a method that returns a value
use a returned value in the calling code

steps.instruction: showDamage prints 12. Now add it to a running total.

points.label: System.out.println
points.text: The method puts 12 on the screen and that is all it does.

points.label: run() never sees the 12
points.text: It cannot add it to anything or compare it.

points.label: what we want
points.text: A method that hands the number BACK, so the caller can use it.

steps.instruction: return hands a value back to whoever called.

points.label: public int damage
points.text: int instead of void: this method hands back a whole number.

points.label: return hits * 3;
points.text: Works out 12 and sends it back. The method ends right there.

points.label: int total = damage(4);
points.text: The call is replaced by 12, which then goes into total.

points.label: damage(4) * 2
points.text: You can use the returned value directly in a bigger expression. This is 12 * 2.

steps.instruction: Printing a value, versus handing it back.

sides.label: void - prints it
int - returns it

points.label: void - prints it
points.text: The 12 reaches the screen and nowhere else.

points.label: int - returns it
points.text: The 12 reaches run(), which adds 100 to it. Only the returned version can be used.

skills: write a method that returns a value

steps.instruction: The return type says what comes back.

points.label: void
points.text: Nothing comes back. A void method cannot be put on the right of an =.

points.label: int
points.text: A whole number comes back, so int total = damage(4); works.

points.label: double, boolean, String
points.text: Any type can be returned. The header and the returned value must agree.

points.label: return ends it
points.text: Nothing after a return runs. It leaves the method immediately.

steps.instruction: What does this print?
steps.why: twice(5) is replaced by the value it returns, 10, and println prints that.
skills: write a method that returns a value

steps.instruction: This should return the total, not print it.

steps.after: A method whose header says int MUST return an int on every path, or it will not compile.
skills: write a method that returns a value

steps.instruction: public TYPE name(params) { return value; }

points.label: the header
points.text: The type before the name is what comes back: public int damage(int hits).

points.label: return
points.text: Sends the value back and ends the method on the spot.

points.label: using it
points.text: A call to a returning method IS its value, so it can go in a variable, an expression, or a println.

points.label: void vs a type
points.text: void does something. A type answers something. Most useful methods answer.

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.

questions.prompt: What does the int in public int square(int n) mean?
opts: The method takes a whole number
The method prints a whole number
The method hands back a whole number
questions.why: The type before the name is the RETURN type. The type in the brackets is the parameter.

questions.prompt: Why return a value instead of printing it?
opts: So the caller can use the value in further work
questions.why: A printed value only reaches the screen. A returned value reaches the caller, which can store it, compare it, or calculate with it.

skills: write a method that returns a value

steps.instruction: Complete the header and the return.
steps.hint: It hands back a whole number, and the keyword for handing back is return.
steps.after: Header type and returned value must match. int in the header, an int returned.
skills: write a method that returns a value

lessons.title: Javadocs and More Methods
objectives: write a Javadoc comment for a method
use @param and @return correctly

steps.instruction: You have written damage(4). In a month, what does the 4 mean?

points.label: damage(4)
points.text: Four what? Hits, seconds, enemies? The name does not say.

points.label: the return
points.text: 12 what? Hit points, gold, percent?

points.label: reading the body
points.text: You can work it out from hits * 3, but only by reading the whole method. That does not scale.

steps.instruction: A Javadoc comment answers those questions above the method.

points.text: Starts with slash-star-star. An ordinary comment starts /* — the extra star is what makes it a Javadoc.

points.label: the first line
points.text: One sentence saying what the method does.

points.label: @param hits
points.text: Names one parameter and says what it means.

points.label: @return
points.text: Says what comes back. A void method has no @return.

steps.instruction: Same program. One of them you can use without reading.

sides.label: undocumented
documented

points.label: undocumented
points.text: To call it safely you must read the body first.

points.label: documented
points.text: The header tells you what to pass and what you get. The body is an implementation detail.

skills: write a Javadoc comment for a method

steps.instruction: /** description @param name what it is @return what comes back */

points.text: Two stars to open. It goes directly above the method it describes.

points.label: @param
points.text: One line per parameter, naming it first.

points.label: @return
points.text: One line, only if the method returns something.

points.label: it is a comment
points.text: Java ignores it when running. It exists for the person reading your code.

steps.instruction: Which tag describes what comes back?
steps.hint: It describes the value the method hands back.
steps.after: @param goes in, @return comes out. @output is not a Javadoc tag.
skills: write a Javadoc comment for a method

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.

questions.prompt: What does a Javadoc comment start with?
questions.why: Two stars. A single star is an ordinary block comment, and // is a line comment.

questions.prompt: A void method needs which tag?
questions.why: void hands nothing back, so there is nothing for @return to describe. Parameters still get documented.

skills: write a Javadoc comment for a method

lessons.title: Strings Methods
objectives: use String methods to inspect text
count positions from zero

steps.instruction: The player typed a name. You need its initial, and its length.

points.label: "Ada Lovelace"
points.text: A String is not just something to print. You can ask it questions.

points.label: the initial
points.text: The first character, for a save-slot icon.

points.label: the length
points.text: To check the name fits on the card.

points.label: built in
points.text: Java gives Strings methods for all of this. You call them ON the String.

steps.instruction: Five String methods, one name.

points.label: name.length()
points.text: 12 - every character including the space.

points.label: name.toUpperCase()
points.text: A new String in capitals. name itself is unchanged.

points.label: name.charAt(0)
points.text: The character at position 0. Counting starts at 0, so this is the A.

points.label: name.substring(0, 3)
points.text: From position 0 up to but NOT including 3, giving "Ada".

points.label: name.indexOf("Love")
points.text: The position where "Love" starts, which is 4. It is -1 if not found.

steps.instruction: Positions start at 0.

points.label: "Ada"
points.text: A is at 0, d is at 1, a is at 2.

points.label: charAt(0)
points.text: The FIRST character. charAt(1) is the second.

points.label: length() is 3
points.text: But the last position is 2. length is a count; positions are 0-based.

points.label: charAt(3)
points.text: Crashes. There is no character at position 3 in a 3-character String.

steps.instruction: What does this print?
steps.why: Position 0 is d, position 1 is u. Counting from zero is the single most common String mistake.
skills: use String methods to inspect text

steps.instruction: substring(start, end) stops BEFORE end.

points.label: substring(0, 3)
points.text: Positions 0, 1, 2 - giving "dun". Position 3 is left out.

points.label: substring(3)
points.text: One argument means "from here to the end", giving "geon".

points.label: why exclusive
points.text: end - start is the length you get. 3 - 0 is 3 characters.

steps.instruction: Get just the first three letters.
steps.hint: The end position is not included, so it equals how many characters you want.
steps.after: substring(0, 3) gives 3 characters. The second number is where to stop, not the last one to keep.
skills: use String methods to inspect text

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code: String s = "hello";

questions.prompt: What is "hello".length()?
questions.why: length() counts characters, and there are five. The last position is 4.

questions.prompt: What is "hello".charAt(0)?
questions.why: Positions start at 0, so charAt(0) is the first character.

skills: use String methods to inspect text

steps.instruction: Your turn: write yell, which shouts any text back.
steps.code: // write yell(String statement): returns the text in capitals
steps.hint: public String yell(String statement) and return statement.toUpperCase();
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 4.5.4, Yelling. yell("hello") returns "HELLO".
skills: use String methods to inspect text

lessons.title: Strings and Characters
objectives: loop through the characters of a String
use Character methods to test a character
read a char as its number

steps.instruction: You can get one character. Now get every character.

points.label: charAt(0)
points.text: One character, at a position you name.

points.label: every character
points.text: Position 0, then 1, then 2... which is a counter going up. You have written that loop already.

points.label: length() and charAt(i)
points.text: length() says where to stop, charAt(i) fetches each one.

steps.instruction: A for loop plus charAt walks the whole String.

points.label: i < word.length()
points.text: Stops at 4, so i takes 0, 1, 2, 3 - exactly the valid positions.

points.label: word.charAt(i)
points.text: Fetches the character at whatever i currently is.

points.label: i <= word.length()
points.text: Would crash on the last pass. There is no character at position 4.

steps.instruction: What does this print?
steps.why: print keeps them on one line, and the loop visits positions 0, 1, 2 in order.
skills: loop through the characters of a String

steps.instruction: charAt gives a char, not a String.

points.label: char first
points.text: charAt returns a char, so it goes in a char box - the type from 3.2.

points.label: 'g'
points.text: Single quotes for a char. "g" with double quotes is a String and will not compare.

points.label: first == 'g'
points.text: char comparison uses ==, unlike Strings which need .equals().

steps.instruction: Every char is secretly a number.

points.label: (int) 'a'
points.text: 97. Casting a char to an int gives the number Java stores it as - its ASCII value.

points.label: (int) 'A'
points.text: 65. Capitals come before lowercase in the table, so they have smaller numbers.

points.label: 'a' > 'A'
points.text: True, because 97 > 65. Chars can be compared with < and > like numbers.

points.label: why it matters
points.text: Testing c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z' for a capital works because those are just number comparisons.

steps.instruction: Stop at the right place.
steps.hint: The last valid position is length() - 1.
steps.after: <= would ask for position 3 in a 3-character String and crash.
skills: loop through the characters of a String

steps.instruction: A backslash gives you characters you cannot type directly.
steps.output:
First Line
Second Line
Make sure to finish your "homework"

points.label: \n
points.text: A new line, in the middle of one String. One println, two lines of output.
A real quote mark. Without the backslash it would end the String early and break.
A single backslash, when you actually want one.

points.label: still one String
points.text: "First Line\nSecond Line" is a single value. The break is inside it.

steps.instruction: The Character class answers questions about a char.

points.label: Character.isUpperCase(ch)
points.text: false, because 'f' is lowercase.

points.label: Character.isDigit(c)
points.text: true for '0' to '9'. This is how you check a character is a digit without comparing numbers yourself.

points.label: Character.
points.text: These belong to the Character class, so the class name goes in front - not ch.isDigit().

points.label: each returns a boolean
points.text: So they drop straight into an if or an &&.

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code: char c = 'a';

questions.prompt: What does (int) 'a' give?
questions.why: Casting a char to int gives its ASCII value, and 'a' is 97. 'A' is 65.

questions.prompt: Which checks whether a char is a digit?
questions.why: It is a method on the Character CLASS, so the class name goes first.

skills: use Character methods to test a character

steps.instruction: Your turn: is this String made only of digits?
steps.hint: Loop through the characters. If any one is NOT a digit, return false straight away. If the loop finishes, return true.

lessons.title: Exceptions
objectives: tell compile, run-time and logic errors apart
name the exception a crash throws

steps.instruction: Three ways a program goes wrong, and only one of them is loud.

points.label: it will not compile
points.text: A missing semicolon or a misspelt name. Java refuses to run it at all.

points.label: it crashes while running
points.text: It compiles fine, then dies partway - dividing by zero, or asking for character 9 of a 4-letter word.

points.label: it runs and is wrong
points.text: No error at all. It just prints the wrong number, and only you can catch it.

points.label: which is worst
points.text: The last one. The other two tell you where to look.

steps.instruction: A compile error stops it before it starts.

points.label: the missing semicolon
points.text: Line 2 does not end. Java cannot tell where the statement stops.

points.label: no output at all
points.text: Not one line runs. There is nothing to run until it compiles.

points.label: reading the error
points.text: It names a line number. Look at that line and the one above it.

steps.instruction: A run-time error compiles, then dies partway.

points.label: "before" prints
points.text: The program really does start. The first line works.

points.label: 10 / hits
points.text: hits is 0, and integer division by zero throws ArithmeticException.

points.label: "after" never prints
points.text: The crash stops everything from that point.

points.label: hits != 0 &&
points.text: Guard it with short-circuiting, from 3.13.

steps.instruction: Match each mistake to what Java does about it.
pairs: no error at all, just a wrong answer
steps.why: Only the first two are exceptions. The third never starts, and the fourth finishes and lies to you.
skills: name the exception a crash throws

steps.instruction: Run-time crashes have names, and the test asks for them.

points.label: ArithmeticException
points.text: Thrown by integer division by zero: 10 / 0.

points.label: IndexOutOfBoundsException
points.text: Thrown by asking for a position that is not there: "hello".charAt(10) when the last position is 4.

points.label: a compile error has no exception
points.text: A missing semicolon never runs, so nothing is thrown. Exceptions only happen to programs that started.

points.label: reading the name
points.text: The exception name tells you what went wrong before you read a single line of your code.

steps.instruction: Which kind of error is each one?

items.text: a loop that runs one time too few

steps.why: Compile errors are caught before running. Run-time errors stop it partway. Logic errors finish and lie to you.
skills: tell compile, run-time and logic errors apart

steps.instruction: A logic error is silent. It just gives the wrong answer.

points.label: expected 5
points.text: The average of 8 and 2 is 5. This prints 9.

points.label: x + y / 2
points.text: Division happens before addition, so it is 8 + 1, not (8 + 2) / 2.

points.label: no error
points.text: It compiled, it ran, it printed a number. Nothing warned you.

points.label: (x + y) / 2
points.text: Brackets force the addition to happen first.

steps.instruction: This averages wrongly. Fix it.
steps.hint: Division runs before addition. Force the addition first.
steps.after: A logic error nothing could have warned you about. Only checking the answer finds these.
skills: tell compile, run-time and logic errors apart

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code: String hello = "hello";

questions.prompt: int x = 3 (no semicolon), then int y = 4; then int sum = x + y; — run-time error, compile error, both, or neither?
questions.why: Java cannot tell where the first statement ends, so it refuses to build the program. Nothing runs, so there is no run-time error to have.

questions.prompt: String hello = "hello"; char last = hello.charAt(10); — which exception?
questions.why: "hello" has 5 characters, at positions 0 to 4. Position 10 is outside the String, and that is exactly what this exception means.

skills: name the exception a crash throws

steps.instruction: Two bugs, both stopping it compiling. Hunt them.
steps.hint: A String needs double quotes, and every statement needs a semicolon.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 4.7.5, Bug Hunter, in miniature - single quotes on a String, and a missing semicolon.
skills: tell compile, run-time and logic errors apart

lessons.title: String Processing
objectives: build up a String inside a loop
loop over characters and decide something about all of them

steps.instruction: Turn "Ada Lovelace" into a save-slot tag: AL.

points.label: the input
points.text: A full name, any length, with a space somewhere in the middle.

points.label: the output
points.text: One String made of the letters that follow the start and the space.

points.label: the shape
points.text: Look at every character; some of them get added to an answer you are building.

points.label: plan first
points.text: Say the steps in English before writing Java. Start empty, walk the name, add what qualifies.

steps.instruction: Start with an empty String and add to it as you go.

points.label: String backwards = ""
points.text: Empty, not null. There is nothing in it yet but it exists and can be added to.

points.label: backwards = backwards + ...
points.text: Take what you have, add one character, put it back. The same shape as total = total + n.

points.label: i = length() - 1; i >= 0; i--
points.text: Walks the positions backwards, so characters arrive in reverse.

points.label: "dlog"
points.text: The accumulator grew one character per pass: d, dl, dlo, dlog.

steps.instruction: The empty start matters.

points.text: A String of zero characters. length() is 0.

points.label: after two adds
points.text: "ab", length 2. Each add makes a new String and reassigns it.

points.label: why not start with a letter
points.text: Anything you start with ends up in the answer. "" is the only safe start.

steps.instruction: What does this print?
steps.why: Each character is put in FRONT of what is already there, so the result comes out reversed even though the loop runs forwards.
skills: build up a String inside a loop

steps.instruction: Collect only the capital letters.
steps.hint: Whatever you start with stays in the answer.
steps.after: Starting with " " would have printed " AL", and starting with "AL" would have printed "ALAL".
skills: build up a String inside a loop

steps.instruction: Convert To Uppercase: shout a String back, one character at a time.
steps.hint: Start result at "". Loop the characters, add Character.toUpperCase(str.charAt(i)) each time, then return result.
steps.after: CodeHS exercise 4.8.6, Convert To Uppercase. Same empty-start pattern as the initials.
skills: build up a String inside a loop

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code:
String out = "";
out = out + "x";

questions.prompt: Why start an accumulator String at ""?
opts: So nothing unwanted appears in the result

steps.output:

pairs: the template a thing is built from
one thing built from a template
the values an object is holding
the methods an object can run

goblin is the class, Monster is the object

steps.instruction: You have never written the Monster class. You did not need to.

points.text: You can use String, Scanner and Math without reading a line of their source. Same idea, smaller class.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to be a client of a class?

To use the class without writing or changing it

opts: The documentation says what each method takes and returns

lessons.title: Writing Classes

write a toString so the object can be printed

steps.instruction: You have used Monster for three lessons. Now build your own.

points.label: Treasure
points.text: A chest item with a name and a value in gold.

points.label: what it needs
points.text: Somewhere to keep those two values, and a way to build one.

points.label: the client is written
points.text: run() already makes a Crown worth 120 and prints it. Your job is the class it needs.

steps.instruction: A class has fields, then a constructor.

points.label: private String name;
points.text: An instance variable. Every Treasure gets its own copy of this.

points.label: private
points.text: Only code inside Treasure can touch it. The client cannot reach in.

points.label: public Treasure(String name, int value)
points.text: The constructor. Same name as the class, and no return type at all.

points.label: this.name = name;
points.text: this.name is the field; name is the parameter. Without this. you would assign the parameter to itself.

steps.instruction: println(object) calls toString().

points.label: public String toString()
points.text: Spelled exactly like that. Java looks for this name.

points.label: System.out.println(crown)
points.text: No .toString() written anywhere, and yet it runs. println asks the object for its String.

points.label: without it
points.text: You would get Treasure@1b6d3586 - the class name and a memory address.

steps.instruction: Two treasures, one class. What prints?
steps.why: Each object holds its own name and value, and toString uses whichever object it was called on.
skills: write a class with private instance variables and a constructor

steps.instruction: The constructor forgot something. Fix it.
steps.hint: name = name assigns the parameter to itself. The field needs this. in front.
steps.after: Without this., the fields stay null and 0 - which is why it printed "null (0 gold)".

steps.instruction: This was meant to be a constructor. One line stops it being one. Tap it.

skills: write a class with private instance variables and a constructor

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.

questions.prompt: What is different about a constructor?
opts: It can only take one parameter
It has the class name and no return type
questions.why: Same name as the class, and no type before the name - not even void.

opts: So printing the object shows something readable
So the object can be created

lessons.title: Writing Classes and Instance Methods
objectives: write instance methods that use and change the fields
tell an instance variable apart from an instance method

steps.instruction: Treasure can be printed. It cannot do anything.

points.label: what it has
points.text: name and value. Instance variables - its state.

points.label: what it does
points.text: Nothing yet, apart from describe itself.

points.label: what we want
points.text: polish() to raise its value, and isRare() to answer a question about it.

steps.instruction: An instance method can use the fields directly.

points.label: public void polish()
points.text: An instance method. No static, so it belongs to one object.

points.label: value = value + 10;
points.text: No dot, no parameter. Inside the class, the fields are just there.

points.label: crown.polish()
points.text: Runs it for the crown, so the crown's value changes and nothing else does.

points.label: 95 then 105
points.text: The same object printed twice, with a changed field in between.

steps.instruction: Data only, or data that can act.

sides.label: client does the work
object does the work

points.text: Every client must know that polishing means +10. Change the rule and you change every client.

points.label: object does the work
points.text: The rule lives in the class. Clients just ask.

skills: write instance methods that use and change the fields

points.label: public boolean isRare()
points.text: Returns a value, so it can go in a println or an if.

points.label: return value > 100;
points.text: Uses the object's own value. The crown is 120, the ring is 45.

points.label: same method, two answers
points.text: Which object you call it on decides the result.

A variable is what the object has; a method is what it does

lessons.title: Getter and Setter Methods
objectives: write a getter that hands a private field out
write a setter that controls what goes in

steps.instruction: The fields are private. The client cannot read them.

points.label: private int value;
points.text: Only Treasure can touch it. That is what private means.

points.label: crown.value
points.text: Will not compile from run(). The client is locked out.

points.label: but it needs the number
points.text: To add up a haul, or compare two treasures.

points.label: the way in
points.text: A method inside the class that hands the value out. That is all a getter is.

steps.instruction: A getter returns a private field.

points.label: public int getValue()
points.text: public so the client can call it; int because that is what it hands back.

points.label: return value;
points.text: The whole body. A getter does nothing else.

points.label: the name
points.text: getSomething is a convention, not a rule. Everyone follows it, so follow it.

points.label: read-only
points.text: The client can now SEE value but still cannot change it.

points.label: setValue(200)
points.text: Accepted. value becomes 200.

points.label: setValue(-50)
points.text: Refused. A treasure cannot be worth minus fifty, so the setter ignores it.

points.label: still 200
points.text: The second print proves the bad value never got in.

points.label: if (newValue >= 0)
points.text: This is the whole point of a setter. A public field could not have refused.

steps.instruction: A public field cannot say no.

sides.label: public field
private + setter

points.label: public field
points.text: Anyone can put anything in it, including nonsense.

points.label: private + setter
points.text: The class decides what counts as a legal value, and keeps deciding forever.

steps.instruction: int is not an object. Sometimes that is a problem.

points.label: int hp = 20;
points.text: A primitive. It holds a number and nothing else - no methods, no dot.

points.label: hp.something()
points.text: Will not compile. There is nothing to reach into.

points.label: Integer
points.text: The object version of int. Same number, but it is a real object with methods.

points.label: why it exists
points.text: Some parts of Java only accept objects. You will meet one in the next unit.

steps.instruction: Integer and Double wrap a primitive in an object.

points.label: Integer wrapped = 20;
points.text: Capital I. Java boxes the 20 into an Integer object automatically.

points.label: Double dw = 2.5;
points.text: Capital D, for doubles. Same idea.

points.label: they print the same
points.text: 20 either way. The difference is what you can DO with it, not what it shows.

points.label: capital letters
points.text: int and double are primitives; Integer and Double are classes. The capital is the tell.

steps.instruction: The same number, with and without methods.

sides.label: int - a value
Integer - an object

points.label: int - a value
points.text: Arithmetic works, and that is all it can do.

points.label: Integer - an object
points.text: Arithmetic still works, AND it has methods like .equals(), plus class constants like MAX_VALUE.

skills: tell a primitive apart from its wrapper class

points.label: Double.parseDouble("2.5")

lessons.title: Method Overloading

steps.instruction: Most potions are standard strength. A few are not.

points.label: new Potion("Elixir", 60)

points.label: two constructors
points.text: Same name - it has to be, a constructor is named after its class - but different parameters.

points.label: Potion(String, int)
points.text: Runs when you pass two arguments.

points.label: Potion(String)
points.text: Runs when you pass one, and fills in 10 itself.

points.label: Java chooses
points.text: By counting and typing the arguments at the call. Nothing else distinguishes them.

points.label: overloading
points.text: The name for this: several methods sharing a name, told apart by their parameters.

steps.instruction: Two names to remember, or one.

sides.label: separate names
one overloaded name

points.text: The caller must remember which name goes with which situation.

points.label: one overloaded name

points.label: different types

points.label: NOT the return type

points.label: NOT the parameter names
points.text: heal(int a) and heal(int b) are the same method twice, and will not compile.

steps.why: One argument, so Java picks Potion(String), which sets healing to 10 itself.

items.text: attack(int a) and attack(int a, int b)

steps.why: Count and types distinguish them. Return type does not - at the call site Java has not got to the return yet. Parameter NAMES do not either; heal(int amount) and heal(int power) are the same method declared twice.
skills: explain how Java chooses which one to run

steps.instruction: Potion has two constructors. This call matches neither.
steps.hint: One constructor takes a name, the other a name and a number. Zero arguments is not on the menu.
steps.after: Overloading gives you the versions you wrote, not every version imaginable. No match means it will not compile.
skills: explain how Java chooses which one to run

public void heal(int amount) { }

lessons.title: Objects vs Primitives
objectives: compare objects with equals and primitives with ==
avoid a null pointer exception

steps.instruction: Two identical potions. == says they are different.

points.label: a == b
points.text: false. Two separate objects were built, and == asks whether they are the SAME object.

points.label: a.equals(b)
points.text: true. equals asks whether their contents match, which is usually what you meant.

points.label: int x == y
points.text: For primitives == compares the values, so it works as expected. Only objects behave this way.

points.label: you saw this in 3.15
points.text: Strings are objects, which is why == failed there too.

steps.instruction: What does == actually compare?
chips: whether it is the same object
rows: whether it is the same object
whether it is the same object
steps.why: Primitives hold their value directly, so == compares values. Object variables hold a reference to a thing, so == compares which thing.
skills: compare objects with equals and primitives with ==

steps.instruction: A primitive is copied. An object reference is shared.

points.label: bump(n)
points.text: Passes a COPY of the 5. The method changes its copy.

points.label: still 5
points.text: run()'s n was never touched.

points.label: objects differ
points.text: Passing an object passes a copy of the REFERENCE, so both point at the same thing and changes are seen by both.

steps.instruction: An object variable can hold nothing at all.

points.label: null
points.text: Means "points at no object". An object field starts this way until you set it.

points.label: calling a method on null
points.text: There is no object to run it, so Java throws a NullPointerException and the program stops.

points.label: where it comes from
points.text: A constructor that forgot this., or a field never assigned. You saw exactly that in 5.11.

points.label: avoiding it
points.text: Set every field in the constructor, and check for null before calling a method on something that might be.

steps.instruction: What does this print?
steps.why: equals compares the characters, which match. == would be unreliable here for exactly the reason in the table.
skills: compare objects with equals and primitives with ==

steps.instruction: It compiles and then dies. The constructor takes a name and forgets it.
steps.hint: An object field starts out pointing at nothing. Something has to put the value in.
steps.after: name still pointed at nothing, so name.length() had no object to run on - a NullPointerException. Setting every field in the constructor is what prevents it.
skills: avoid a null pointer exception

opts: Calling a method on a variable that points at no object
questions.why: null means no object, so there is nothing to run the method on. Division by zero is ArithmeticException, from 4.7.

skills: avoid a null pointer exception

lessons.title: Inheritance
objectives: write a subclass with extends and super
tell an IS A relationship from a HAS A relationship

steps.instruction: A Boss is a Monster with one extra thing.

points.label: what it shares
points.text: A name, hp, and the ability to roar. Identical to Monster.

points.label: what it adds
points.text: A title, and the ability to enrage.

points.label: copying the class
points.text: Would duplicate name, hp and roar, and any fix to roar would then need doing twice.

points.label: IS A
points.text: A Boss IS A Monster. That relationship is what inheritance is for.

steps.instruction: Copy the shared parts, or inherit them.

sides.label: copied
sides.output:
Grendel roars!
Grendel the Terrible enrages!

sides.label: inherited
sides.output:
Grendel roars!
Grendel the Terrible enrages!

points.label: copied
points.text: name, hp and roar exist twice. Fixing roar means fixing it in both places.

points.label: inherited
points.text: Boss adds only what is new. roar is written once, in Monster.

skills: write a subclass with extends and super

steps.instruction: extends takes everything the parent has.
steps.output:
Grendel roars!
Grendel the Terrible enrages!

points.label: class Boss extends Monster
points.text: Boss is now a Monster as well, and gets its fields and methods.

points.label: b.roar()
points.text: Not written anywhere in Boss. It came from Monster.

points.label: super(name, hp)
points.text: Calls Monster's constructor to set up the inherited half. It must be the FIRST line.

points.label: getName()
points.text: Boss cannot touch Monster's private name directly, so it uses the inherited getter.

steps.instruction: super(...) runs the parent constructor first.

points.label: super(name, hp);
points.text: Hands the shared values up to Monster, which stores them.

points.label: first line
points.text: It must come before anything else in the constructor. The parent half is built first.

points.label: leaving it out
points.text: Java tries to call a no-argument Monster() instead, and there is not one, so it will not compile.

points.label: private stays private
points.text: A subclass inherits private fields but cannot name them. Getters are how it reaches them.

steps.instruction: IS A, or HAS A?
steps.why: If one thing IS a kind of the other, subclass it. If one thing merely HAS the other, store it as a field.
skills: tell an IS A relationship from a HAS A relationship

steps.instruction: Everything already inherits from Object.

points.label: Object
points.text: The class at the top of every hierarchy in Java. You never write extends Object - it is automatic.

points.label: toString()
points.text: Comes from Object. That is why println(anything) works even before you write your own.

points.label: Treasure@1b6d3586
points.text: Object's version of toString. Writing your own in 5.4 replaced it.

points.label: Boss extends Monster extends Object
points.text: Three levels of hierarchy, and you only wrote one of them.

steps.instruction: roar is not written in Boss. What happens?
steps.why: Boss inherited roar from Monster, so calling it on a Boss runs Monster's version using the Boss's own name.
skills: write a subclass with extends and super

steps.instruction: Boss sets its own field before the parent has been built.
steps.hint: The inherited half has to exist before the subclass adds to it.
steps.after: super(...) must be the very first line of the constructor. Java builds a Boss from the Monster outwards.
skills: write a subclass with extends and super

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.

questions.prompt: What does super(name, hp) do?
questions.why: It builds the inherited half of the object, and must be the first line of the subclass constructor.

questions.prompt: Which is an IS A relationship?
questions.why: A Boss IS A kind of Monster, so it subclasses it. A Hero merely HAS a sword, so the sword is a field.

skills: tell an IS A relationship from a HAS A relationship

objectives: use abstract to stop a class being instantiated

points.text: What would it even be? Monster is a category, not a creature.

points.label: every monster attacks
points.text: But each one does it differently, so Monster cannot say how.

points.label: abstract
points.text: Marks a class as "a category only". Java then refuses to let anyone build one.

Green Slime splatters you.
Grendel unleashes a shockwave.

points.label: getName() is normal

sides.label: not abstract
abstract

points.text: The meaningless object is impossible, and every real monster must say how it attacks.

steps.instruction: Two jobs: forbid, and require.

points.label: abstract class
points.text: Cannot be instantiated. It exists to be extended.

points.label: abstract method
points.text: Has no body. Any concrete subclass must provide one.

points.label: not the same
points.text: An abstract class can have zero abstract methods and still refuse to be built.

points.label: design
points.text: Put in the parent what every child shares. Leave abstract what each must decide for itself.

points.text: Legal, because a Boss IS A Monster.

points.text: m says Monster. The object is a Boss. Which attack() runs?

points.text: And neither IS A the other, so inheritance does not apply.

points.label: but both open
points.text: You want one method that can open either.

points.label: an interface
points.text: A promise that a class provides certain methods, with no family relationship at all.

steps.output:
The chest creaks open.
The door swings wide.

points.label: interface Openable
points.text: A list of method signatures and nothing else. No fields, no bodies, no constructor.

points.label: void open();

points.label: class Chest implements Openable
points.text: implements, not extends. Chest promises to have open().

points.label: unrelated classes
points.text: Chest and Door share nothing except the promise.

steps.instruction: An interface can be a parameter type, like a parent class.
steps.output:
The chest creaks open.
The door swings wide.

points.label: useIt(Openable thing)
points.text: Accepts anything that implements Openable, whatever its class.

points.label: the same payoff as 5.15
points.text: Polymorphism again, but across unrelated classes rather than a family.

points.label: adding a Gate
points.text: Would work with useIt immediately, as long as it implements Openable.

sides.label: abstract class
interface

points.label: abstract class
points.text: Can hold fields, constructors and finished methods. A class extends exactly one.

points.label: interface
points.text: Only the method list. A class can implement as many as it likes.

skills: compare an interface with an abstract class

steps.instruction: Which one allows it?
rows: be used several times by one class
declare a method with no body

steps.after: A class extends one class and implements as many interfaces as it likes.

Be used as a parameter type
