lessons.title: What are Data Structures?
objectives: name the four data structures and what each is for
choose the right structure for a job

steps.instruction: Three monsters took three variables. Twenty would take twenty.

points.label: hp1, hp2, hp3
points.text: Numbered by hand. There is no way to loop over them.

points.label: twenty monsters
points.text: Twenty variables, and a sum twenty terms long.

points.label: a data structure
points.text: One variable that holds many values, which you CAN loop over.

steps.instruction: Four of them, and each is for a different job.

points.label: array
points.text: A fixed number of values, all the same type. Fastest and simplest. Size is set when you make it.

points.label: ArrayList
points.text: Like an array, but it grows and shrinks. Use it when you do not know how many yet.

points.label: 2D array
points.text: A grid - rows and columns. For maps, boards and tables.

points.label: HashMap
points.text: Pairs. Look a value up by a name rather than a number, like "gold" to 5.

steps.instruction: Which structure fits the job?
pairs: each item name to its price
steps.why: Fixed count means an array. Unknown or changing count means an ArrayList. A grid means 2D. Looking up by a name rather than a position means a HashMap.
skills: choose the right structure for a job

steps.instruction: The same three numbers, in one variable.

points.label: int[] hp
points.text: One variable holding three ints. The square brackets make it an array.

points.label: hp.length
points.text: How many it holds. The program can ask, which it never could with hp1, hp2, hp3.

points.label: hp[0]
points.text: The first one. Positions start at 0, exactly like String characters in 4.5.

points.label: this lesson
points.text: Just the shape of them. Arrays properly start next lesson.

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.

questions.prompt: Which structure should you use when you do not know how many items there will be?
questions.why: An array has a fixed size once created. An ArrayList grows and shrinks as you add and remove.

questions.prompt: What is a HashMap for?
opts: Looking a value up by a name instead of a number
questions.why: It stores pairs, so you ask for "gold" rather than position 3.

skills: name the four data structures and what each is for

steps.instruction: Fixed size, or grows?

items.text: loot you pick up as you play

steps.why: An array is created at one size and stays there. An ArrayList changes size as the program runs.
skills: choose the right structure for a job

steps.instruction: Your turn: put four scores in one variable and print how many there are.
steps.hint: int[] scores = {10, 20, 30, 40}; then .length and [0].
steps.after: One variable, four values, and the program can count them itself.
skills: name the four data structures and what each is for

lessons.title: Introduction to Arrays
objectives: make an array and read it by index
change an item and find the length

steps.instruction: One name, many slots, numbered from zero.

points.label: int[] hp
points.text: A row of int slots under a single name.

points.label: numbered
points.text: The first slot is 0, not 1. Same counting as String positions in 4.5.

points.label: fixed
points.text: Once made, an array cannot grow. Its length never changes.

steps.instruction: Two ways to make one.

points.text: Values listed up front. The length becomes 3 automatically.

points.label: new String[3]
points.text: Three empty slots, filled in later.

points.label: names[1]
points.text: null - never assigned. Empty object slots start null; empty int slots start 0.

points.label: both are arrays
points.text: The difference is only whether you know the values yet.

steps.instruction: An index reads a slot, and can be assigned to.

points.label: hp[0]
points.text: 20 - the first slot.

points.label: hp[2]
points.text: 8 - the third and last, because 3 slots are numbered 0, 1, 2.

points.label: hp[1] = 50;
points.text: An index on the LEFT of = writes to that slot instead of reading it.

points.label: hp.length
points.text: 3. No brackets - it is a field, not a method, unlike String's length().

steps.instruction: Three slots, numbered from zero.

questions.prompt: hp[0]
questions.why: The first slot. Counting starts at 0.

questions.prompt: hp[2]
questions.why: The third and last, because 3 slots are numbered 0, 1, 2.

questions.prompt: hp.length
questions.why: How many slots there are - not the last index, which is 2.

skills: make an array and read it by index

steps.instruction: What does this print?
steps.why: a[2] is read first (15), then written into slot 0. The right-hand side is worked out before the assignment.
skills: change an item and find the length

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.

questions.prompt: What is the index of the LAST item in an array of length 3?
questions.why: Indexes start at 0, so a length of 3 means 0, 1, 2. The last index is always length - 1.

questions.prompt: How do you find how many items an array holds?
questions.why: For an array it is a field with no brackets. String uses length() WITH brackets, and ArrayList uses size().

skills: change an item and find the length

steps.instruction: Set the last slot without counting by hand.
steps.hint: Length 3, last index 2. What do you subtract?
steps.after: length - 1 is the last index, whatever the size. Writing 2 would break the moment the array changed.
skills: change an item and find the length

steps.instruction: Your turn: swap in a new first monster and report the size.
steps.hint: hp[0] = 100; then print hp[0] and hp.length.
steps.after: The length stayed 3. Assigning to a slot changes what is in it, never how many there are.
skills: make an array and read it by index

lessons.title: Using Arrays
objectives: traverse an array with a for loop
explain what happens past the end of an array

steps.instruction: Adding three by hand is fine. Adding twenty is not.

points.label: hp[0] + hp[1] + hp[2]
points.text: Works, and stops working the moment the array is a different size.

points.label: the loop already exists
points.text: You wrote for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) in 3.9. An index is exactly what i is.

points.label: i < hp.length
points.text: Makes the loop fit any array, whatever its size.

steps.instruction: The counter and the index are the same number.

points.label: int i = 0
points.text: Starts at the first index, not 1.

points.label: i < hp.length
points.text: Stops at 3, so i takes 0, 1, 2 - exactly the valid indexes.

points.label: hp[i]
points.text: A different slot each pass: 20, then 45, then 8.

points.label: i <= hp.length
points.text: Would try hp[3] and crash. Use < with length, always.

steps.instruction: hp[3] on a 3-slot array crashes.

points.label: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
points.text: Thrown at run time when the index is past the end. You met its cousin in 4.7 with charAt.

points.label: why 3 is past the end
points.text: Three slots are numbered 0, 1, 2. There is no slot 3.

points.label: it compiles fine
points.text: Java cannot know at compile time what i will be, so this is a run-time error, not a compile one.

points.label: i < hp.length
points.text: Keeps you inside. Every off-by-one here ends in this exception.

steps.instruction: How many times does the body run?
steps.why: length is 4, so i takes 0 to 3 and every slot prints once.
skills: traverse an array with a for loop

steps.instruction: Two names can point at the SAME array.

points.label: int[] b = a;
points.text: Does NOT copy the array. Both names now refer to the same one.

points.label: b[0] = 99;
points.text: Changes the single array that both point at.

points.label: a[0] is 99
points.text: Even though a was never assigned to. This surprises everyone once.

points.label: an array is an object
points.text: From 5.12, an object variable holds a reference, not the thing itself.

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.

questions.prompt: What happens when a program reads hp[3] here?
opts: It throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at run time
questions.why: Three slots are numbered 0 to 2. Java checks at run time and throws.

questions.prompt: int[] b = a; then b[0] = 99. What is a[0]?
questions.why: b = a copies the reference, not the contents, so both names see the same array.

skills: explain what happens past the end of an array

steps.instruction: Make the loop cover every slot and no more.
steps.hint: The last valid index is length - 1, so the loop must stop BEFORE length.
steps.after: <= would try a[3] and throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
skills: traverse an array with a for loop

steps.instruction: Your turn: find the strongest monster in the party.
steps.hint: Start best at hp[0], then loop from i = 1 replacing best whenever hp[i] is bigger. Same shape as Find the Minimum in 3.11.
steps.after: Exactly the pattern from Find the Minimum, over an array instead of three variables.
skills: traverse an array with a for loop

lessons.title: Enhanced For Loops
objectives: traverse an array with an enhanced for loop
say when the enhanced form does not fit

steps.instruction: Most loops never use i for anything except hp[i].

points.label: for (int i = 0; i < hp.length; i++)
points.text: Three pieces of ceremony to look at every item.

points.label: hp[i]
points.text: The only place i appears. The index itself is not interesting.

points.label: the enhanced for
points.text: Hands you each value directly, with no counter at all.

steps.instruction: Same total, less ceremony.

sides.label: indexed for
enhanced for

points.label: indexed for
points.text: You manage the counter, the bound and the lookup yourself.

points.label: enhanced for
points.text: n IS the value. No index to get wrong, so no out-of-bounds is possible.

skills: traverse an array with an enhanced for loop

steps.instruction: for (Type name : array) reads as "for each".

points.label: String item
points.text: The type of ONE element, not of the array.
Read it as "in". For each item in loot.

points.label: no counter
points.text: No i, no length, no brackets. It visits every element in order.

points.label: read only
points.text: Assigning to item changes the copy, not the array. That is the main limit.

steps.instruction: When the enhanced form does not fit.

points.label: you need the position
points.text: Printing "3. Cup" needs the index, so use the indexed form.

points.label: you need to change the array
points.text: hp[i] = 0 works. Assigning to the loop variable does not.

points.label: you need part of it
points.text: Enhanced always visits everything, start to finish.

points.label: otherwise
points.text: Prefer the enhanced form. Fewer moving parts, no off-by-one.

steps.instruction: Does the array change?
steps.why: n is a copy of each element. Changing the copy leaves the array untouched, which is why writes need the indexed form.
skills: say when the enhanced form does not fit

steps.instruction: loot holds Strings. This does not compile.
steps.hint: The type in front of the loop variable is the type of ONE element.
steps.after: String[] holds Strings, so each item is a String. The type never matches the array, only what is inside it.
skills: traverse an array with an enhanced for loop

steps.instruction: Which loop does each job need?
steps.why: The enhanced for gives you values, not positions, and the value is a copy. The moment you need to know WHERE you are, or to write back into the array, you need the index.
skills: say when the enhanced form does not fit

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code: for (int n : hp) { }

questions.prompt: What type goes before the name in for (___ n : hp)?
questions.why: The variable holds one element at a time, so for a String[] it is String.

questions.prompt: When must you use the indexed for instead?
opts: When you need the position, or need to change the array
questions.why: The enhanced form gives you values, not positions, and its variable is a copy.

skills: say when the enhanced form does not fit

steps.instruction: Your turn: count the party members still standing.
steps.hint: for (int n : hp) then an if inside counting the ones above 0.
steps.after: No index anywhere, so there was no off-by-one to make.
skills: traverse an array with an enhanced for loop

lessons.title: ArrayList Methods
objectives: create an ArrayList and add to it
use size, get, add and remove

steps.instruction: You do not know how much loot the player will find.

points.label: int[] loot = new String[?]
points.text: An array needs its size up front. You do not have one.

points.label: guessing big
points.text: new String[100] wastes 97 slots and still breaks at 101.

points.label: ArrayList
points.text: Starts empty and grows as you add. Size is a running total, not a decision.

steps.instruction: Create empty, then add.

points.label: ArrayList<String>
points.text: The angle brackets say what it holds. A list of Strings.

points.label: new ArrayList<String>()
points.text: Starts empty - size 0, no slots reserved.

points.label: loot.add("Crown")
points.text: Appends to the end and the size goes up by one.

points.label: loot.get(0)
points.text: Reads by position, still counting from 0. A method, not square brackets.

steps.instruction: Square brackets, or methods.

sides.label: array
ArrayList

points.label: array
points.text: loot[0], loot.length, and a size fixed at 2 whether or not you filled it.

points.label: ArrayList
points.text: loot.get(0), loot.size(), and a size that is however many you actually added.

skills: create an ArrayList and add to it

steps.instruction: add, get, size, remove, set.

points.label: remove(1)
points.text: Takes out "Ring". Everything after it shifts down, so "Cup" moves from 2 to 1.

points.label: set(0, "Tiara")
points.text: Replaces what is at 0. Unlike add, it does not change the size.

points.label: size() is now 2
points.text: Three added, one removed. The list tracks it for you.

points.label: removing renumbers
points.text: Everything after the removed item moves down. That catches people inside loops.

steps.instruction: The enhanced for works on an ArrayList too.

points.label: for (String item : loot)
points.text: Identical to the array version from 6.4.

points.label: the indexed form
points.text: Works too, but uses loot.size() and loot.get(i) instead of length and brackets.

points.label: no size to manage
points.text: The loop covers whatever is in the list at the time.

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code: ArrayList<String> loot = new ArrayList<String>();

questions.prompt: How do you find how many items an ArrayList holds?
questions.why: Arrays use .length with no brackets, Strings use .length(), and ArrayLists use .size().

questions.prompt: Why choose an ArrayList over an array?
opts: The number of items can change while the program runs
questions.why: An array is fixed at creation. Arrays hold objects perfectly well - that is not the difference.

skills: use size, get, add and remove

steps.instruction: Ask the list how big it is.
steps.hint: Three different collections, three different spellings. This one is a method.
steps.after: array.length, string.length(), list.size(). Worth memorising as a set.
skills: use size, get, add and remove

steps.instruction: These are numbers, and remove takes a number. Careful.
steps.why: remove(1) removed the item AT INDEX 1 - the 20 - not the value 1. The list is now [10, 30], so index 1 holds 30. With an ArrayList of numbers this is very easy to get wrong.
skills: use size, get, add and remove

steps.instruction: It prints both items and then falls over.
steps.hint: size() is 2, and the last index is 1. Which comparison stops one short?
steps.after: Same off-by-one as an array, with size() in place of length. <= always asks for one item too many.
skills: use size, get, add and remove

steps.instruction: Your turn: collect loot, drop one, and report what is left.
steps.hint: remove(1) takes out the Ring. Then size() and an enhanced for over what is left.
steps.after: Cup shifted from index 2 to 1 when the Ring went. The list renumbered itself.
skills: use size, get, add and remove

lessons.title: Arrays vs ArrayLists
objectives: choose between an array and an ArrayList
say how an ArrayList is built on an array

steps.instruction: Two collections. The party roster, and the loot bag.

points.label: the party
points.text: Four heroes, decided at the start and never changing. An array fits.

points.label: the loot bag
points.text: Empty at first, grows all game, and things get dropped. An ArrayList fits.

points.label: the question
points.text: Not which is better. Which matches what the data does.

steps.instruction: The same three items, both ways.

sides.label: array
ArrayList

points.label: array
points.text: Square brackets, .length, and a size fixed forever at creation.

points.label: ArrayList
points.text: get/set/size, and add and remove change the size as you go.

skills: choose between an array and an ArrayList

steps.instruction: Which one can do it?
steps.why: An array is a fixed block with bracket syntax and can hold int directly. An ArrayList grows, uses methods, and stores objects — an int goes in as an Integer, from 5.8.
skills: choose between an array and an ArrayList

steps.instruction: An ArrayList is an array underneath.

points.label: an array plus a count
points.text: It keeps an ordinary array, plus a count of how many slots are actually used.

points.label: add
points.text: Writes into the next free slot and raises the count.

points.label: running out
points.text: When the array is full it makes a BIGGER one and copies everything across. That is how it "grows".

steps.instruction: An ArrayList cannot hold int. It holds Integer.

points.label: ArrayList<Integer>
points.text: Capital I. ArrayList<int> will not compile - it stores objects only.

points.label: scores.add(10)
points.text: Java boxes the 10 into an Integer for you, from 5.8.

points.label: int first = scores.get(0)
points.text: And unboxes it back on the way out.

points.label: int[] scores
points.text: An array holds the ints directly, with no boxing at all.

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code:
int[] a = new int[3];
ArrayList<Integer> b = new ArrayList<Integer>();

questions.prompt: When should you choose an array over an ArrayList?
opts: When the number of items is known and fixed
questions.why: A fixed count means an array is simpler and cheaper. An unknown or changing count means an ArrayList.

questions.prompt: Why can an ArrayList not hold int directly?
opts: It stores objects, so ints are boxed into Integer
questions.why: ArrayList<int> does not compile. ArrayList<Integer> does, and Java boxes and unboxes automatically.

skills: say how an ArrayList is built on an array

steps.instruction: An ArrayList cannot hold a primitive.
steps.hint: It stores objects. int is not one - but it has an object twin with a capital letter.
steps.after: Java boxes the 30 into an Integer going in and unboxes it coming out, so you write ordinary ints either side.
skills: choose between an array and an ArrayList

steps.instruction: One of these counts with a field. The other with a method.
steps.hint: An array is built into the language and exposes length directly. An ArrayList is a class, so it has to be asked.
steps.after: No brackets on length, brackets on size(). Mixing them up is one of the commonest compile errors in this unit.
skills: choose between an array and an ArrayList

steps.instruction: Your turn: pick the right one and total it.
steps.hint: The count is fixed and known, so an array literal is the simpler fit.
steps.after: A fixed roster is exactly what an array is for. Reaching for an ArrayList here buys nothing.
skills: choose between an array and an ArrayList

lessons.title: Additional Loop Examples
objectives: traverse an ArrayList with an indexed loop
remove items safely while looping

steps.instruction: Drop every fallen member from the party list.

points.label: the list
points.text: An ArrayList of hp values, some of them 0.

points.label: the job
points.text: Remove every 0, leaving the survivors.

points.label: removing while looping
points.text: Removing while looping forwards skips items, and this is where it bites.

steps.instruction: The indexed loop over a list uses size() and get().

points.label: i < hp.size()
points.text: size() where an array used .length.

points.label: hp.get(i)
points.text: get(i) where an array used [i].

points.label: same shape
points.text: The loop from 3.9 is unchanged. Only the two spellings differ.

points.label: when you need it
points.text: The enhanced for is nicer for reading, but it gives no index and cannot remove.

steps.instruction: Removing forwards skips the next item.

points.label: two zeros in a row
points.text: Removing index 0 shifts the second zero DOWN into index 0.

points.label: i++ then runs
points.text: So i becomes 1, and the zero now sitting at 0 is never looked at.

points.label: size is 2, not 1
points.text: One zero survived. The loop believed it had checked everything.

points.label: no error
points.text: This is a logic error from 4.7 - it runs happily and gives the wrong answer.

steps.instruction: Loop backwards and the shifting stops mattering.

points.label: i = hp.size() - 1
points.text: Start at the last index and count down.

points.label: why it works
points.text: Removing shifts only the items AFTER i, and those have already been checked.

points.label: size is 1
points.text: Both zeros gone. Only the 8 remains.

points.label: remove backwards
points.text: Removing inside a loop: go backwards.

steps.instruction: Forwards removal again. What size prints?
steps.why: Removing index 0 shifts the second x down to 0, then i becomes 1 which is no longer less than size 1. One survives.
skills: remove items safely while looping

steps.instruction: This is meant to remove every 0 and does not. Tap the line to blame.
steps.why: Removing at i pulls everything after it down one place, and then i++ moves on anyway - so whatever slid into position i is never examined. The loop and the if are both fine. It is removing while going forwards that breaks it.
skills: remove items safely while looping

steps.instruction: Complete the backwards loop.
steps.hint: It starts at the last index and has to reach 0.
steps.after: Going down, a removal only shifts items you have already passed, so nothing gets skipped. Both zeros go.
skills: remove items safely while looping

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code: for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) { }

questions.prompt: What replaces .length and [i] when looping an ArrayList?
questions.why: Arrays use .length and brackets; ArrayLists use size() and get().

questions.prompt: Why remove items by looping backwards?
opts: Removing shifts later items down, and those are already checked
questions.why: Going forwards, the shift moves an unchecked item into the index you just passed.

skills: remove items safely while looping

steps.instruction: Your turn: drop every fallen member and count the survivors.
steps.hint: Start at size() - 1 and count down with i--, removing when the value is 0.
steps.after: Forwards would have left one zero behind and printed 3.
skills: remove items safely while looping

lessons.title: The List Interface
objectives: declare a variable by the List interface
accept List as a parameter type

steps.instruction: A method that prints a list should not care which kind it is.

points.label: ArrayList
points.text: One way of being a list. There are others in Java.

points.label: List
points.text: An interface - the promise from 5.17. It lists add, get, size, remove and the rest.

points.label: ArrayList implements List
points.text: So every ArrayList already IS a List.

steps.instruction: Declare by the interface, build with the class.

points.label: List<String> loot
points.text: The variable type is the promise, not the implementation.

points.label: new ArrayList<String>()
points.text: You still need a real class to build an object. An interface cannot be instantiated.

points.label: everything else
points.text: add, get and size are unchanged - they are on the interface.

points.label: swapping implementation
points.text: Swapping to another List implementation later means changing one line, not every line.

steps.instruction: A List parameter accepts any list.

points.label: show(List<String> items)
points.text: Takes the interface, so it works with any class that implements List.

points.label: the same argument as 5.15
points.text: Polymorphism again. There the parent was a class; here it is an interface.

points.label: ArrayList would work too
points.text: But it would then refuse every other kind of list for no reason.

points.label: accept the general type
points.text: Accept the most general type that does the job.

steps.instruction: Tied to one class, or open to any list.

sides.label: ArrayList parameter
List parameter

points.label: ArrayList parameter
points.text: Only ever accepts an ArrayList, even though it uses nothing specific to one.

points.label: List parameter
points.text: Accepts any List. Identical body, wider reach.

skills: accept List as a parameter type

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code: List<String> a = new ArrayList<String>();

questions.prompt: Why declare the variable as List rather than ArrayList?
opts: The code then depends on the promise, not one implementation
questions.why: Swapping the implementation later changes only the new on the right of the =.

lessons.title: 2D Arrays (Matrices or Grids)
objectives: make a 2D array and read it by row and column
find the number of rows and columns

steps.instruction: The dungeon map is rows AND columns.

points.label: a 1D array
points.text: A single row of rooms. Fine for a corridor, useless for a floor plan.

points.label: a grid
points.text: Needs two numbers to find a square: which row, which column.

points.label: a 2D array
points.text: An array whose elements are themselves arrays. That is all it is.

steps.instruction: Two sets of brackets, two indexes.

points.label: String[][]
points.text: Two pairs of brackets: an array of arrays.

points.label: the inner braces
points.text: Each { } is one row. Two rows here, two columns each.

points.label: map[0][1]
points.text: Row 0, column 1 - "room". Row first, then column, both counting from 0.

points.label: map[1][1]
points.text: Row 1, column 1 - "exit". The bottom right.

steps.instruction: One length for rows, another for columns.

points.label: grid.length
points.text: 2 - the number of ROWS, because the outer array holds two inner arrays.

points.label: grid[0].length
points.text: 3 - the number of columns, which is the length of one row.

points.label: grid[0]
points.text: Is itself an ordinary 1D array. That is why it has its own .length.

points.label: rows first
points.text: The outer number is always rows. Getting this backwards is the usual bug.

steps.instruction: Row first, then column.

questions.prompt: grid[0][0]
questions.why: First row, first column.

questions.prompt: grid[1][2]
questions.why: Second row, third column.

questions.prompt: grid.length
questions.why: Two rows. The columns are grid[0].length, which is 3.

skills: find the number of rows and columns

steps.instruction: What does this print?
steps.why: Three inner arrays means three rows, and each holds two values, so two columns.
skills: find the number of rows and columns

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code: int[][] grid = new int[4][7];

questions.prompt: How many rows and columns does new int[4][7] have?
questions.why: The first number is the outer array - the rows. The second is the length of each row.

questions.prompt: What IS a 2D array in Java?
opts: An array whose elements are arrays
questions.why: Which is why grid[0] is itself an array with its own .length.

skills: make a 2D array and read it by row and column

steps.instruction: Your turn: build a 2x2 map and read one square.
steps.hint: Bottom right is row 1, column 1. Rows are map.length.
steps.after: Row then column, both from 0. That order never changes.
skills: make a 2D array and read it by row and column

lessons.title: Traversing 2D Arrays
objectives: traverse a 2D array with nested loops
use nested enhanced for loops on a grid

steps.instruction: Printing the whole map means visiting every square.

points.label: one loop
points.text: Walks one row. It cannot reach the second.

points.label: a loop inside a loop
points.text: The outer picks a row, the inner walks that row's columns.

points.label: row 0, then row 1
points.text: Row 0 fully, then row 1 fully. Left to right, top to bottom.

steps.instruction: Outer loop rows, inner loop columns.

points.label: r < grid.length
points.text: The outer loop counts rows: r takes 0 then 1.

points.label: c < grid[r].length
points.text: The inner counts columns IN THAT ROW. Using grid[r] not grid[0] handles rows of different lengths.

points.label: grid[r][c]
points.text: Row r, column c. The inner loop runs completely for each single r.

points.label: println() after
points.text: Outside the inner loop but inside the outer, so it ends each row.

steps.instruction: The inner loop finishes before the outer moves on.

points.label: r = 0
points.text: c runs 0, 1, 2 - printing 1, 2, 3. Then the line ends.

points.label: r = 1
points.text: c runs 0, 1, 2 again - printing 4, 5, 6.

points.label: 2 x 3 = 6 visits
points.text: 2 rows x 3 columns = 6 visits. Nested loops multiply.

points.label: swapping them
points.text: Looping columns outside and rows inside prints the grid sideways.

steps.instruction: The enhanced form nests too.

points.label: for (int[] row : grid)
points.text: Each element of a 2D array IS a 1D array, so the loop variable is int[].

points.label: for (int n : row)
points.text: Then an ordinary enhanced for over that row.

points.label: no indexes at all
points.text: Shorter, and no off-by-one possible.

points.label: read-only, as in 6.4
points.text: Same as 6.4 - no positions, and you cannot write back into the grid.

steps.instruction: How many times does the inner body run?
steps.why: 3 rows times 2 columns. Nested loops multiply rather than add.
skills: traverse a 2D array with nested loops

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code:
for (int r = 0; r < grid.length; r++)
  for (int c = 0; c < grid[r].length; c++)

questions.prompt: What does the OUTER loop count?
questions.why: grid.length is the number of inner arrays, which are the rows. The inner loop walks one row.

questions.prompt: In for (int[] row : grid), why is the type int[] and not int?
opts: Each element of a 2D array is itself a 1D array
questions.why: A 2D array is an array of arrays, so one element is a whole row.

skills: traverse a 2D array with nested loops

steps.instruction: Make the inner loop follow the row it is on.
steps.hint: The inner loop should measure the row it is currently on, not always the first one.
steps.after: g[r].length is right even when rows have different lengths. g[0].length only works if they are all equal.
skills: traverse a 2D array with nested loops

steps.instruction: Your turn: total every number in the grid.
steps.hint: Nested enhanced for: the outer gives each int[] row, the inner gives each int in it.
steps.after: 1+2+3+4+5+6 is 21, and no index appeared anywhere.
skills: traverse a 2D array with nested loops

lessons.title: HashMaps
objectives: store and look up pairs in a HashMap
handle a key that is not present

steps.instruction: Two lists that have to stay lined up.

points.label: names
points.text: ["Ana", "Ben", "Cy"] - position 0 is Ana.

points.label: scores
points.text: [90, 75, 60] - position 0 is Ana's score. The link is the index, and nothing enforces it.

points.label: looking up Ana
points.text: Walk the names until you find her, remember WHERE, then read that slot of the other list.

points.label: what you actually want
points.text: To look a score up BY THE NAME. Not by a position you had to go hunting for.

steps.instruction: A HashMap stores pairs: a key, and the value it points at.

points.label: HashMap<String, Integer>
points.text: Two types now: the key type, then the value type. Names point at scores.

points.label: put("Ana", 90)
points.text: Files 90 under the key "Ana". No index anywhere.

points.label: get("Ana")
points.text: Hands back 90. It does not search - it jumps straight there.

points.label: Integer, not int
points.text: Same rule as ArrayList. A map holds objects, so int becomes Integer.

steps.instruction: A key that was never put returns null.

points.label: get("Zoe")
points.text: null - not 0. The map does not invent a score for someone it has never heard of.

points.label: why that bites
points.text: int score = scores.get("Zoe"); crashes. There is no number to unwrap.

points.label: containsKey
points.text: Asks first, without reading. Gives back true or false.

points.label: getOrDefault("Zoe", 0)
points.text: Reads, but substitutes 0 when the key is absent. Usually what you meant.

steps.instruction: Keys are unique, and they are not kept in order.

points.label: put("Ana", 100)
points.text: Ana was already a key, so this REPLACES 90. It does not add a second Ana.

points.label: keySet()
points.text: Every key, which you can run an enhanced for over.

points.label: Zoe went in last
points.text: and came out first. The map does not keep the order you added things in.

points.label: so do not rely on it
points.text: If the order matters to you, you wanted a list.

steps.instruction: What is the size at the end?
steps.why: Putting "a" twice overwrote the first value. Two distinct keys, so size is 2.
skills: store and look up pairs in a HashMap

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code:
HashMap<String, Integer> ages = new HashMap<String, Integer>();
ages.put("Ana", 15);

questions.prompt: What does ages.get("Ben") return?
questions.why: An absent key gives null. It only crashes if you then try to store that null in an int.

questions.prompt: Why HashMap<String, Integer> rather than HashMap<String, int>?
opts: A map stores objects, and int is not one
questions.why: Same rule as ArrayList - the collection holds objects, so the wrapper type Integer is used.

skills: store and look up pairs in a HashMap

steps.instruction: Count how many times each word appears.
steps.hint: The first time a word is seen it is not in the map yet, so reading it must not give back null.
steps.after: get would return null on the first "red", and null + 1 crashes. getOrDefault starts it at 0.
skills: store and look up pairs in a HashMap

steps.instruction: Your turn: print Ben's score, or 0 if he has none.
steps.hint: One method does both the check and the read.
steps.after: Ben was never put, so the default 0 came back instead of null.
skills: store and look up pairs in a HashMap

lessons.title: Binary
objectives: convert between binary and decimal
explain why computers store data in binary

steps.instruction: A wire is either carrying current or it is not.

points.label: two states
points.text: On or off. That is everything the machine physically has.

points.label: one wire
points.text: Can tell you 0 or 1. Two things.

points.label: so how do you get 13?
points.text: You use more than one wire, and you give each one a different worth.

steps.instruction: Each position is worth double the one to its right.

points.text: Reading right to left: 1, 2, 4, 8. Doubling every step.
Take the 8, take the 4, skip the 2, take the 1.
is 13. A binary digit only ever says "take this one" or "skip it".

points.label: decimal does the same
points.text: 347 is 3 hundreds, 4 tens, 7 ones. Same idea, ten symbols instead of two.

steps.instruction: Java converts both directions for you.

points.label: parseInt("1101", 2)
points.text: Read this text as a number written in base 2. Gives 13.

points.label: the 2
points.text: The base. parseInt("1101") with no base reads it as one thousand one hundred and one.

points.label: toBinaryString(13)
points.text: The other direction - the digits Java would need to hold 13.

points.label: the number never changed
points.text: 13 and 1101 are the same amount written two ways. Binary is notation, not a different value.

steps.instruction: Every extra digit doubles what you can hold.

points.label: 8 digits, all 1
points.text: 128+64+32+16+8+4+2+1 = 255. That is the biggest 8 digits can say.

points.label: 8 digits is a byte
points.text: 256 different values, counting from 0 to 255.

points.label: 256 needs a ninth
points.text: Just like 99 to 100 in decimal - you run out and grow a column.

points.label: why it matters
points.text: A type is a fixed number of digits. That is what makes an int run out.

steps.instruction: What prints?
steps.why: Worth 4 2 1. Take the 4, take the 2, skip the 1. 4 + 2 = 6.
skills: convert between binary and decimal

steps.instruction: Match each binary number to its value.
steps.why: A single 1 followed by zeros is just that place value. Adding a 1 on the end adds one more.
skills: convert between binary and decimal

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code: Integer.toBinaryString(n)

questions.prompt: How many different values can 4 binary digits hold?
questions.why: Each digit doubles it: 2, 4, 8, 16. They count from 0 to 15, which is 16 values.

questions.prompt: Why does a computer use binary rather than decimal?
opts: Hardware has two reliable states, on and off
questions.why: Ten distinguishable voltage levels would be fragile. Two is easy to tell apart, so two symbols it is.

skills: convert between binary and decimal

steps.instruction: Print 10 as binary.
steps.hint: You have a number and you want the digits. Which direction is that?
steps.after: 8 + 2 = 10, so take the 8, skip the 4, take the 2, skip the 1.
skills: convert between binary and decimal

steps.instruction: Your turn: print the value of binary 10011.
steps.hint: Either add up the place values yourself, or let parseInt do it with base 2.
skills: convert between binary and decimal

lessons.title: Ethical Issues Around Data Collection
objectives: judge whether a data practice needs consent
explain how combining fields reveals more than any one field

steps.instruction: A step counter needs your steps. Look at what it actually takes.

points.label: what it needs
points.text: A step count. That is the whole product.

points.label: what it takes
points.text: Location every few minutes, so it can measure distance.

points.label: and keeps
points.text: Timestamps. When you left, when you got back, every day for two years.

points.label: the gap
points.text: Nothing here is stolen. Every field has a reason. The reasons are not the problem.

steps.instruction: One field is boring. Fields together are not.

points.label: a location
points.text: A point on a map. Could be anyone.

points.label: locations at 3am, every night
points.text: Where you sleep. That is your home address.

points.label: plus 9am on weekdays
points.text: Your school or your workplace.

points.label: aggregation
points.text: The conclusion was never in any single row. It came from putting rows side by side.

steps.instruction: "We remove your name" does less than it sounds.

points.label: the claim
points.text: The name column is deleted, so the data is anonymous.

points.label: ZIP code, date of birth, sex
points.text: Three fields nobody thinks twice about. Together they narrow most people down to a single person.

points.label: re-identification
points.text: Match those three against any public list that does have names, and the name is back.

points.label: anonymous is relative
points.text: Anonymous is not a property of one table. It depends on every other table that exists.

steps.instruction: Sort each one.

items.text: The step counter stores your steps so you can see last week
It keeps your location history to measure distance walked
It sells that location history to an advertiser
It uses your data to improve its step-counting accuracy
It shares data with a research hospital, with names removed
It keeps your full history after you delete your account

steps.why: The line is rarely the data itself. It is whether the use is the one you agreed to, and whether you could say no.
skills: judge whether a data practice needs consent

steps.instruction: Match each term to what it means.
pairs: Combining separate fields to learn something no single field said
Putting names back onto data that had them removed
Collecting only the fields the feature actually needs
Off until the user turns it on
On until the user finds the setting and turns it off
steps.why: Opt-in and opt-out collect the same field. They differ only in who has to act, and that decides what most people end up with.
skills: judge whether a data practice needs consent

steps.instruction: Two worth being sure about.
steps.code: // no code for this one

questions.prompt: An app collects your contacts to "improve your experience". What is the strongest objection?
opts: It should be opt-out instead of opt-in
The purpose is too vague to agree or disagree with
Contacts are never useful to an app
questions.why: You cannot consent to a purpose you cannot picture. A reason that covers everything is not a reason.

questions.prompt: A dataset has no names, but has ZIP, birth date and sex. Is it anonymous?
opts: No - those three together often identify one person
Only if it has fewer than 1000 rows
Yes, as long as it is not made public
questions.why: That is exactly the combination re-identification attacks use.

skills: judge whether a data practice needs consent

steps.prompt: A school app records which websites each student visits during class, so teachers can see who is off task. Name one thing about it you think is reasonable, and one change you would require before it ships.
steps.rubric: Credit an answer that (a) acknowledges a legitimate purpose - the teacher does have a reason to know whether students are working - and (b) names a concrete, specific change rather than a general objection. Strong changes: limit it to class time only, show teachers a status rather than a full browsing list, delete the logs after a set period, tell students plainly that it is on, collect only whether a site is on-task rather than which site. Weak answers reject it outright with no purpose acknowledged, or ask vaguely for "more privacy" with nothing specific.
skills: judge whether a data practice needs consent
steps.instruction: Write a few sentences. There is no single right answer here.
Four questions to ask about any feature you build.

points.label: What does it need?
points.text: Not what would be useful. What breaks if you leave the field out.

points.label: How long?
points.text: Data kept forever is data that leaks eventually.

points.label: Who else sees it?
points.text: Every extra copy is another place it can go wrong.

points.label: Could they say no?
points.text: And still use the thing. If not, it was not really a choice.

objectives: choose the right structure for a job

steps.instruction: Nothing new here. Six checks across the whole unit.

points.label: what it covers
points.text: Arrays, enhanced for, ArrayList, removing while looping, 2D grids, HashMaps.

points.label: how to use it
points.text: If one goes wrong, the lesson it came from is the one to go back to.

steps.instruction: What prints?
steps.why: length is 4, so the last valid index is 3. a[a.length] would be the error.
skills: make an array and read it by index
explain what happens past the end of an array

steps.instruction: What does the array hold at the end?
steps.why: n is a copy of the element. Assigning to it changes the copy, not the array. That is what the enhanced form cannot do.
skills: traverse an array with an enhanced for loop
say when the enhanced form does not fit

questions.why: The outer length is the number of rows. grid[0].length measures one row, which is the number of columns.

A queue of students that grows and shrinks all day

choose between an array and an ArrayList
